t: by touch. By touching it.
and by carrying. By carrying it.
and by tent. As explained below in halakhah 10.
seven-day impurity. One needs seven days to become pure from it (see Hilchot Parah 11:1).
impurity of carrying, from the oral tradition. The law that a corpse defiles by carrying was learned from the tradition of the Sages.
if a carcass, which is evening-impurity. One who is defiled by it is impure only until he immerses and evening comes after his immersion (see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 10:1).
a corpse all the more so. That it should defile by carrying, since it is more severe, defiling with seven-day impurity.

and if a carcass... so too the corpse etc.. Just as with a carcass the impurity of touching and of carrying are equal, so we learn that with a corpse the impurity of touching and of carrying are equal.
but a law of the Torah. Even though it is not stated explicitly in the Torah.

just as it was silent about the prohibition of a daughter etc.. The prohibition of relations with one's daughter is not mentioned explicitly in the Torah, only the prohibition of relations with one's son's daughter or daughter's daughter, and from this they learned that a daughter is forbidden (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 2:6).

and it was silent about the prohibition of eating meat with milk etc.. Likewise the prohibition of eating meat and milk cooked together is not stated explicitly in the Torah, only the prohibition of cooking them together (see Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 9:1-2).
even in his tongue. For the purpose of receiving impurity the tongue is considered an external organ, although for other purposes it is considered internal (see Hilchot Parah 12:1).
but if a person thrust impurity into a spindle. Stuck the impurity into a wooden implement used for spinning.
into the woman's womb. Into her uterus.
the swallower is not defiled as one who touches. But he is defiled as one who carries (see below halakhah 8, and Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 3:4).
for inner touching is not touching. See also below 25:12; Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 5:9.
the membrane over the wound. The scab on the wound.
is like the skin of the flesh as regards touching impurities. Although for other purposes it is not considered like the skin of the flesh (see Hilchot Mikva'ot 2:1).
and the hair of a minor. The fine hair in a minor's flesh that later falls out.

and the like, of the things that interpose on the body. When these are stuck to the body of the person immersing, they count as an interposing item between him and the water and prevent the immersion (for the list of interposing items see Hilchot Mikva'ot chapter 2. Halakhah 14 there states that dirt of excrement does not interpose; and see Kesef Mishneh, who writes that the correct reading here is: 'and likewise dirt of excrement or mud, of the things that do not interpose on the body, and likewise scabs of excrement, of the things that interpose on the body, are not like the skin of the flesh').
but only from its airspace. If impurity entered its cavity it becomes impure even if the impurity did not touch it, and it does not become impure by touch as other vessels do.
as will be explained in Hilchot Kelim. 13:1.
and this is a great principle in the matter of impurities etc.. See also below 5:7.
even if there was a stone between him and her. One that does not receive impurity.
a beam resting on the wall. So that the middle of the beam lies on the thickness of the wall and its two ends are on the two sides of the wall.
and on one side of it is a corpse or carcass and the like. On one of its ends lies something that defiles by carrying.
he pulled the other end toward the ground until he lifted the impurity. He pulled that end of the beam downward, causing the opposite end, on which the impurity lies, to rise.
or dragged the impurity along the ground. With some object, even without touching it.
for this one is certainly a carrier. In these cases he moved the impurity from its place to another place, and not only the menstruant.
one who carries inside the hidden places. When the impurity is in the inner places of his body, such as inside the nose, ear or mouth.
for although touching there is not touching. As above, halakhah 3.
one who carries there is a carrier. See Hilchot Matmei Mishkav UMoshav 8:5.
for once it reached his belly he is neither touching nor carrying. Therefore, although the impurity defiled him while it was in his mouth, it does not defile him from then on.
and if he immersed, he is pure. See Hilchot Mikva'ot 2:8.
placed on his hand. He is carrying them in his hand.

whether the person or the vessel spreads over it etc.. If a person or a vessel, even the smallest, is above the corpse or beneath it, or is with it under one tent, it becomes impure with tent-impurity.
touched the lintel. The beam above the doorway.

and joined his hand with the lintel. He placed his hand against the lintel from outside so that it extends the thickness of the lintel. He becomes impure because his hand is considered part of the tent that spreads over the corpse, even though it did not enter the space under the lintel (Merkevet HaMishneh).
touched the threshold. Touched the outer side of the step at the entrance of the house, parallel to the lintel.
from a handbreadth down, near the ground, he is pure. He is considered as touching the ground (and see also below 6:8).

and from a handbreadth up he is impure; and it seems to me that this is rabbinic. For by Torah law the outer side of the threshold is not considered part of the house with respect to impurity (see below 25:6).
and a gentile does not defile by tent. See also below 9:4; Hilchot Evel 3:3.
and this is a tradition. A tradition of the Sages.
and it says in the war of Midian. Regarding the men who were defiled by corpse impurity from those slain in the Midianite war.
and it does not mention a tent there. From which we learn that a gentile does not defile by tent.
that gentiles should be like zavim in all their matters. That they defile in all the ways a zav defiles (for the details of the law see Hilchot Matmei Mishkav UMoshav 2:10).
and among all kinds of living beings, there is nothing that becomes impure etc.. By the words of the Torah.
and upon the persons. All persons are included, even minors.
and this is if he was born at nine months. After nine months of pregnancy.
an eight-month baby. One born after eight months of pregnancy.

is like a stone. This newborn is not classed as a living person because he is destined to die, and he is considered inanimate, neither alive nor dead (see also Hilchot Milah 1:13; Hilchot Shabbat 25:6).
megayad. One whose veins have been cut (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 1:7).
even if two signs were slaughtered in him. The windpipe and the gullet; all of these are near death.
for it says, 'the soul of a man who dies'. This implies only when his soul has died and not before.
his neck was broken and most of the flesh with it. The neck vertebrae were broken along with most of the flesh on them.
this one defiles. For all of these are considered as if their soul had already departed and they had died (see also Hilchot Shechitah 3:19).
even though he still twitches in one of his limbs. For even after death the limbs may move slightly.
even though his limbs are not yet bound with sinews. He is still only flesh, without sinews and bones.
for any human soul. Any soul at all, including nefalim (stillborn).
an olive's bulk of the flesh of a corpse. Flesh of a corpse the size of an olive.

flesh that dissolved and became putrid fluid. Part of a corpse's flesh that dissolved and became liquid (through heat, disease or decay), and also liquid parts of the body (such as the lubricating fluids in the joints) that come out when the flesh begins to rot.
provided that it congealed. That after death the fluids congealed again.
for if it congealed, it is known that it is from his flesh. Then it defiles like the flesh of a corpse.

it does not defile, since perhaps it is his phlegm and mucus. Since it did not congeal, we assume it comes from secretions originating in the lungs (due to a cold and the like), which are not considered part of the corpse's body and therefore do not defile like his flesh.

the beginning of a person's formation is an olive's bulk. The stage at which it has the basic form of a person (compare Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 10:3, and see Tiferet Yisrael, Boaz, Oholot 2:5, who discusses the relationship between the two places).
is like a complete corpse. Even though the person himself is still alive.
even a small limb of a one-day-old infant. That does not contain an olive's bulk.
for it says etc.. A proof that a limb from a living person defiles.
one slain by the sword. A person killed by a blow of the sword.
from the oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages.
a limb that the sword cut off. That was severed from the person by a sword or the like.
they are like the rest of the flesh. That which separates from a living person is pure, as stated below.
flesh on which healing could grow in a living person, and it would heal and be whole. That if this limb were attached to a living person, its flesh would heal and make up the missing part.
and if not, it defiles by touch and by carrying, but does not defile by tent. Since it is not in its natural form.
and flesh that separates from a living person. Without bone.
its bone is lacking. Part of its bone is missing.
it defiles like a complete corpse. By touch, by carrying and by tent.
it is like the other bones of the dead that have no flesh on them. And it defiles by touch and carrying only (below 3:2).
it raises healing from outside. Through the marrow, the flesh outside the bone heals.
this is like a complete corpse. Like a limb of a corpse, which defiles by touch, by carrying and by tent.
if it contained rattling marrow. That dried up and was displaced from its place within the cavity and cannot raise healing from outside.
this defiles by tent. Like the law of an olive's bulk of flesh, which defiles by touch, by carrying and by tent.
even though the bone is closed on all sides. And it is impossible to spread over the marrow inside.
impurity breaks upward and breaks downward. Like the law of anything that defiles by tent where there is no space of a handbreadth in its place.
as will be explained. Below 7:5.
the limb and the flesh hanging on a person. That are about to be torn off but are still attached to his body.
even though they cannot return to life, they are pure. As long as the person is alive they are not considered detached.

the flesh is pure. Like flesh that separates from a living person (above halakhah 3). For after death this flesh and limb are considered as having been torn off during his life (for this principle see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 2:5).
pure. Like things that separate from a whole living person (above halakhah 3).
and they defile according to their measure. Flesh at an olive's bulk (above halakhah 1) and bone at a barleycorn's bulk (below halakhah 9).
a man has two hundred and forty-eight limbs. They are listed in the Mishnah, Oholot 1:8.
and likewise an extra finger. A person who has an additional finger.
if it is counted on the back of the hand. If it is in the same row as the other fingers.

it counts toward the majority of the limbs. Its status is equal to the two hundred and forty-eight limbs of a person, so it affects the number needed for a majority of the corpse's bones, as explained below, halakhah 8.

and its impurity is rabbinic. By Torah law it does not defile at all, since it is not considered part of the body (like fingernails, which do not defile, as below 3:13; Reshit Bikkurim, Bekhorot 45:1).
it is like the other limbs. Although it is not counted with them, since it has a nail, its law regarding impurity is like that of the other two hundred and forty-eight limbs.

so that terumah and sacrificial foods not be burned because of its impurity. For impurities that are a rabbinic decree, terumah and sacrificial foods are not burned on account of them (see also Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 7:4; Hilchot Kelim 17:5).
if the form of human bones is recognizable in them. That they are bones in which it is evident that they are human bones.
for I call them 'a human bone'. As it says, 'and whoever touches... a corpse or a human bone' (Numbers 19:16); from this, such bones defile like a complete corpse.
the shizrah. The spinal column.
it is like the other bones. Their law will be explained below, halakhah 9.
and if it lacks a sela's worth. If a piece the size of a large coin is missing, a person cannot live with a loss of that size (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 2:3; Hilchot Shechitah 10:5).
all of them combine to a sela's worth. Even though they are scattered over the whole skull.
such as his two shins and one thigh. Which in size make up most of the person's height.
such as one hundred and twenty-five bones. Which are most of a person's limbs, the total being two hundred and forty-eight (above halakhah 7).
even if this person had extra limbs. In which case the stated number is not a majority of his bones.
or was missing limbs. In which case even fewer than the stated number is a majority of his bones.
for it counts toward the number. Its status is equal to the two hundred and forty-eight limbs of a person, so it affects the number needed for a majority of the corpse's bones.
as we explained. Above, halakhah 7.
a quarter-kav. A volume of about 300 cc.
a bone the size of a barleycorn. A bone with the volume of a grain of barley.
from the tradition. The tradition of the Sages.
a corpse whose bones rotted in the grave and became dust. After the moisture of the corpse is gone, its bones crumbled and became like ash (Commentary on the Mishnah, Eduyot 6:3; Oholot 2:1).

because it is impossible to touch all of it, as it is not one body. Since the crumbs are not joined to one another, one who touches some of them is not defiled, because he did not touch the amount that defiles.
even if he kneaded it with water. Mixed it with water so that it would join.
it is not a joining. Because ash is not something that can be kneaded, it is not considered joined by kneading (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 2:2; and see Hilchot Shabbat 8:16).
a revi'it. A quarter of a log, about 75 cc.
even the tamtzit of blood. The clear liquid that comes out of blood as it congeals, whose color differs slightly from that of blood.
blood of nechirah. Blood that comes out of a person who is being put to death, before his soul departs.
even half a revi'it from a living person and half after death. For the mixture does not contain a majority of the corpse's blood that defiles.
all the blood in it is pure. Even if most of the blood in the hollow is from blood that came out after death.

for each drop, one after another, is nullified in the blood that came out from the living. Each drop of impure blood that falls into the hollow is nullified, being a minority, by the pure blood (for this principle see also Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 16:28).
as will be explained in its place. Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 15:8.
as long as the impurity is within it. As long as the corpse is buried in it.
defiles by touch and by tent like a corpse, by Torah law. It does not defile by carrying because it is attached to the ground.

provided it is built and sealed. As long as it is open it is not a grave. In addition, it must have a space of a handbreadth by a handbreadth by a handbreadth in height in order to defile on all its sides (below 7:4).
but one who sets up vessels etc.. That are not built like a grave but are detached, movable things.
or stones. Even though they do not receive impurity.
therefore if he dragged the golel with ropes etc.. For all of these are ways of becoming impure through heset (shifting), which is included in impurity of carrying (above 1:7).
and things that support the dofek. That are placed beside it and it leans on them.
perhaps there is in it a bone the size of a barleycorn. Which defiles by touch and by carrying.
lands of the nations. Lands other than the Land of Israel.
because of the bones that they are not careful about. They treat the dead lightly and bury them anywhere (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 2:3).
as will be explained. Below 9:12; the details of their laws are explained below, chapters 10-11.
these defile by touch, by carrying and by tent etc.. All of which were explained above in chapter 2.
a limb from a living person whose flesh is lacking. It does not have enough flesh to raise healing. But if its bone is lacking, it does not defile at all (above 2:3).
and a limb from a corpse whose flesh or bone is lacking. Ibid., halakhah 4.
and a spine that is lacking. Ibid., halakhah 8.
and does not have a quarter-kav of bones. It does not have the measure of a quarter-kav of bones (ibid., halakhah 9).
and a skull that is lacking. Ibid., halakhah 8.
and a single bone even the size of a barleycorn. Ibid., halakhah 9.
and the land of the nations and a beit hapras. Ibid., halakhah 16.
the golel and the dofek. Above 2:15.
the decay. Ibid., halakhah 11.

the impurity of a quarter-kav of bones by tent. Where one spread over a quarter-kav of bones that has neither most of the structure nor most of the number (above 2:9; but for half a kav of bones a nazirite must shave; see Hilchot Nezirut 7:2).
and the impurity of a revi'it of blood. As long as it does not have the measure of half a log, which defiles by Torah law (ibid.).
and the impurity of a limb without proper flesh... from a corpse. For example, where it has no bone the size of a barleycorn (Kesef Mishneh).

for a nazirite does not shave because of them. A nazirite who became impure with corpse impurity loses the days of his naziriteship that he observed and must shave his hair and bring offerings (Hilchot Nezirut 6:3); if he became impure with one of these impurities, although he is impure with seven-day impurity, his naziriteship is not nullified.
as we explained in Nezirut. 7:1, 7:6-7.
and one is not liable because of them for entering the Temple etc.. See Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 3:13-14.
in a coffin of marble or glass and the like. Materials that do not decay.
and it must be entirely whole. Although decay defiles at the measure of a full double handful (above 2:11), it must come from a complete corpse.
its decay is not impure, because the decay of clothing... mixes with the decay in its formation. Since they mix with the decay as it is forming, this is not the decay that defiles.
rust of metal. Flakes of rust from metal.
and decay that defiles, with which any amount of dust was mixed, remains in its impurity. Because the mixing occurred after the decay was formed.
but one who was slain has no decay. Since he was killed and blood left him, he is not a complete corpse, and therefore his decay does not defile (Hilchot Nezirut 7:3).
or they cut his hair or his nails and buried them with him. For they are not considered part of the corpse when they are not attached to it (below, halakhah 13).
they have no decay. Their decay does not defile, since other things are mixed in it.
he ground all of it and left it until it decayed. He did not grind it to the stage of actual decay but only to dust, and it finished decaying after the grinding.
this is in doubt. Whether it is considered as having decayed by itself or not (for these laws see also Hilchot Nezirut 7:4).
a full double handful and more. The measure of a full double handful plus a little more.
earth smeared with the fluid of a corpse and its blood. It does not contain the measure of blood and fluid that defile (above 2:1, 2:12), and it does not defile by itself.
this defiles by carrying and by tent. But it does not defile by touch, like decay itself (above 2:11).
a corpse that was burned and its skeleton remains, namely the spine and the ribs. For the spine and ribs still look like their shape although they were burned.
defiles like a complete corpse. By touch, carrying and tent.
a shafir merukam. The membrane of the fetus at the start of its formation, which already has human form (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 10:3). It defiles like any nefel (above 2:1).
that he mixed it. Mixed it well.
that crumbled and became like flour. That dried out so much that it crumbles into fine ash like flour.
and likewise the worms that are generated from the flesh of a corpse. In the process of decay.
and we already explained. Above 2:5.
whether a carcass or a creeping thing. See Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 1:4.
like his flesh. It defiles at an olive's bulk like a complete corpse (see above 2:1).

and if he fully tanned it or walked on it for the time needed for tanning. He tanned the hide, or trampled it with his feet for the length of time suitable for tanning hides, which is the time it takes to walk four mils (see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 1:9, 4:8).
this is pure by Torah law. It is no longer considered a corpse.
a decree, so as not to accustom etc.. For this act harms human dignity.

the skin that comes opposite a person's face when he is born. The placenta in which the fetus lies (Tosafot, Bekhorot 7b). Some explain that it means an additional membrane covering the fetus's face, which is not the placenta itself (Rabbenu Gershom there).
because it is like a discharge etc.. These things are not part of the person and therefore do not defile (for a further law that follows from this see Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 4:20).
since their stock is replaced. These parts of the body are replaced, unlike the rest of the body's parts, which are fixed in a person from the day he is born.
and at the time of their attachment, everything is impure. What is attached to the body is like the body (above 1:3).

everything in the house becomes impure. Since the hair is attached to the corpse, it is considered as if the corpse itself were in the house and it defiles what is in it by tent-impurity (see above 1:10-11).
any fluid that comes out of the corpse. The liquids secreted from it.
as we explained. Above 2:12.
just as they decreed regarding liquids that come out of all impure things. That all liquids that come out of impure things are impure (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 10:4; and see ibid. 7:2).
it defiles at a revi'it. Like the blood of a corpse (see above 2:12).

because it is like congealed blood. Since the liver is full of blood, it is considered as if it were clotted, congealed blood. But as long as it has not dissolved, its law is like that of a corpse's flesh, which defiles at an olive's bulk (Arukh HaShulchan HaAtid 9:11).

and a limb from a living person that is lacking any amount of its bone. Since its bone is lacking, even though it has proper flesh it is pure, because flesh from a living person does not defile by itself (above 2:3).
and likewise a skull of two corpses. That was assembled from two different corpses.
but only by touch and carrying, like all the other bones. See above 2:9.

even from one man, if it was divided in two, it is pure. For this is not a limb in its natural form (above 2:3). And it is pure even from tent-impurity (Mishnah Acharonah, Oholot 3:1; Arukh HaShulchan HaAtid 10:6).
and a full double handful of decay from two corpses. That each decayed separately and were not buried together (see above 3:5).
for each of them has decay. Each has the status of decay according to the definitions explained above, 3:4.
because they did not match in their measures. See also Hilchot Tumat Ochlin 4:11.

it defiles by carrying. One who carries this bone that was divided carries the measure that defiles (as for touch-impurity, the commentators disagree; see Chasdei David on the Tosefta, Oholot 4:3, and Tiferet Yisrael, Boaz, Oholot 2:7, and others).
that they were ground fine and none of them has a bone the size of a barleycorn. They were all ground until they were smaller than the volume of a barleycorn.
and flattened it and stuck it together. He flattened the pieces and stuck them together into one body.
for human joinings are not a joining. Therefore one who touches part of it has not touched the measure that defiles at once.
that he melted it. He turned it into liquid (such as the fat).
if it was separated and he melted it, it is pure. And it does not defile by touch, since human joinings are not a joining.
that most of its vertebrae were scraped away. They were peeled off but not entirely lacking; if they were, the spine does not defile by tent even if only one vertebra is missing (above 2:8).
even though its skeleton remains. The spinal column still exists.
crushed. Broken into pieces.
for the grave combines it. This is a special law of a grave (see Minchat Chinuch 263:10).
that were divided. And each small part is less than the measure that defiles by tent.
the tent combines them. What spreads over them combines them into the measure that defiles.
and brought part of it in. Part of the bone.
the house became impure. The people and vessels inside the house became impure with tent-impurity, as if the flesh itself had entered there.
the house is impure. Because the tent combines them into the measure of an olive's bulk.
for human joinings are not a joining. Therefore the bones are not considered joined to the flesh (and the bones themselves do not defile by tent).
the house is pure henceforth. What enters the house after the revi'it of blood was absorbed in it is pure.
the house is pure. From now on, since it was not found, it is reasonable to assume that animals ate it (Riko).
that was spilled in the open air. Outside the house, in a place with no tent over it (see Tosafot Yom Tov, Oholot 3:3).
and this is a low place like a hollow. A depression in which the blood rests in one place.
and the one who spreads over it spread over part of it, he is impure. In these cases all the blood is considered joined.

spilled on the threshold on a slope, either inward or outward. The blood was spilled on the threshold at the entrance of the house, which sloped toward the house or toward the outside (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.).

for the blood did not rest on the threshold. Therefore, although the house spreads over all of it, it does not become impure, since as long as the blood is moving it does not defile by tent (see ibid.).
this garment defiles by touch, by carrying and by tent. Since a revi'it of blood comes out through laundering, it is not considered absorbed.
and it is like a garment that touched a corpse. Which has seven-day impurity and does not defile by tent or by carrying (below 5:13).
and he brings water according to its measure. According to the amount of water in which the garment was laundered.
from the water of the mixture. From the other waters that were poured into the revi'it of blood.
but one who touches half an olive's bulk or carries half an olive's bulk. In a way that he does not spread over it.
whoever comes into the tent. This implies any person.
and all that is in the tent. This implies all vessels.

and you shall wash your clothes on the seventh day. Said of those returning from the war with Midian who were defiled by a corpse. From this we learn that the clothes they wore are also impure with seven-day impurity.
impure with evening-impurity. Impure until he immerses and the sun sets after his immersion (see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 10:1).
and the soul that touches. A person who touched one impure through a corpse.
rabbinic. An enactment of the Sages.
and as if this second one had touched the corpse itself. Since he touches a person who is attached to the corpse.
regarding terumah and sacrificial foods. That he is forbidden to eat terumah and sacrificial foods, and if he touches them they become impure.
for a nazirite. If he became impure from a corpse he loses the days of his naziriteship and must shave his hair and bring offerings (Hilchot Nezirut 6:3).
and for one who makes the Pesach offering. If he became impure from a corpse, the Pesach offering is not slaughtered for him and he is deferred to the Second Pesach (Hilchot Korban Pesach 6:2).
he is impure only with evening-impurity. Like a person who touches a primary source of impurity (see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot, ibid.).
whether by touch or by tent. But not by carrying, since vessels do not become impure through carrying (above 1:9).
from the oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages.
for the sword is like the corpse. One who touches it is like one who touches the corpse itself.
vessels that are washed. Other vessels that are purified in a mikveh (except clay vessels).
he says. In the war with Midian.
one who kills a person with a sword and the like. In which case the person touches a vessel that touches a corpse.
and you shall wash your clothes on the seventh day. For these clothes touched a person who was defiled through the sword that touched the corpse.
both are impure with seven-day impurity. The first vessels and the second vessels.
the third. One who touches the second vessels.
the fourth. One who touches these vessels that touched the person.

but to make liable to karet for entering the Temple or for eating sacrificial foods. An impure person who deliberately enters the Temple or eats sacrificial foods is liable to karet (Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 3:12; Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 18:13).
as a law of the Torah. See above, halakhah 2.
as it says, 'and whatever the impure person touches shall be impure'. From this we learn that by Torah law even one who touches a person impure through a corpse is called impure.
as we explained in Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash. 3:15 (and see Hilchot Nezirut 7:8 for the law of a nazirite who became impure through vessels that touched a corpse).
words of tradition. A tradition of the Sages.
for it is a primary source. Of impurity.
and the second, who touches it, is a first. One who touches a primary source of impurity is called a first-degree impurity (below, halakhah 8).

a clay vessel that touched a corpse. For example, corpse impurity entered into it, and not that it touched it from outside, since a clay vessel does not receive impurity from its outer side (below 6:3).
or was with it in an impure tent. For impurity in a tent enters it through its opening (ibid.).
for a clay vessel never becomes a primary source of impurity. Only a first-degree impurity (see also Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 10:8).
and this is a law of the Torah even though it is a tradition. It is not stated explicitly in the text but is received by tradition.
any primary source of impurity. For the list of primary sources of impurity see Commentary on the Mishnah, introduction to Seder Taharot.
offspring of the impurities. First-degree impurity and below.
and one who touches the second is called a third. This applies only to terumah and sacred things; but with unconsecrated food, a second does not make a third (see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 11:1-4).
and one who touches the third is called a fourth. This applies only to sacred things, but not to terumah or unconsecrated food (ibid.).
all are called offspring of impurity. Because they are derived from the primary source of impurity (Commentary on the Mishnah, Pesachim 1:6).
whether people or vessels. But not foods and liquids, which never become a primary source of impurity (Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 10:9).
as we explained. Above, halakhot 4-5.
and he is the first degree of impurity. For he touched a primary source of impurity.
as we explained. Above, halakhot 4-5.
the land of the nations and a beit hapras. See above 2:16.
or by carrying them. But not by tent, for they do not defile by tent.
blood of trampling. Ibid., halakhah 13.
and golel and dofek. Ibid., halakhah 15.
or by their tent. But not by carrying, for they do not defile by carrying.

and likewise garments that become impure because of these with seven-day impurity. The garments that become impure because of this person, since every person with seven-day impurity makes garments impure with seven-day impurity (above, halakhah 3).
as it says, 'and he shall sprinkle upon the tent'. From this we learn that the tent becomes impure from a corpse, since it requires sprinkling of the purification water to purify it.
or sackcloth. Which is woven from the hair of animals (see Hilchot Kelim 1:12).
or a wooden vessel. That is, what comes from wood, which is only flax, as he explains below (Kesef Mishneh).
only woven fabric and hide are called a tent, like the Tabernacle. The curtains of the Tabernacle were made of woven fabric, and its covering was made of hide.
and the like. Things made of wood that are not vessels.
or if it was of bone or of metal. For example, they are not vessels and do not receive impurity.
and needless to say, if it was a building. That is attached to the ground and made of stones that do not receive impurity even as vessels (Hilchot Kelim 1:6).
only flax. It is the only material that comes from wood that is called a tent, since the Tabernacle was woven from it (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shabbat 3:2).
even though they are like a corpse in defiling others etc.. As above, halakhah 3.
as we explained. Above 1:2.
'a person who dies in a tent'. This implies a person specifically, and not other things.
it does not defile a lying or sitting place beneath it. It does not defile with midras impurity like a zav and the like (see Hilchot Matmei Mishkav UMoshav, chapters 6-7).
nor madaf above it. It does not defile vessels that are above it and do not touch it (unlike a zav and the like, who defile by madaf; see ibid. 6:3).
whether a vessel etc.. The law is the same in all cases: only what touches the corpse directly, and what touched that, are impure for seven days, as explained below.
the garment that touches it and the second garment that touched the garment that touched it are both impure with seven-day impurity. As above, halakhah 4.

and the fourth, and from the fourth downward and from the fourth upward, are all pure. For the third garment does not defile them, since it is an offspring of impurity and does not defile garments (above, halakhah 7).
unlike those who defile a lying and sitting place. These are the zav and zavah, the menstruant and the woman after childbirth.
as will be explained in its place. Hilchot Matmei Mishkav UMoshav 6:3, 6:5.

when there was no crushed impurity there. When the impurity is crushed it defiles everything above and below it even when it does not touch it (for the definition of this concept see below 7:5, 12:1). The case here is, for example, where the garment or vessel touching the corpse is long, and the other garments or vessels lie above or below it, not opposite the corpse, so that impurity reaches them only through touch (Mishnah Acharonah, Zavim 4:6).
nor tent-impurity. There is no tent spreading over the corpse and over the garments or vessels that would bring the impurity upon them.

or a stone separated between it and the vessels. The corpse lies on the stone, and the garments are folded beneath it at a handbreadth above the ground, so that the stone above them becomes a tent over them and interposes against the impurity (see below 16:7, 17:4). In this case none of the garments become impure, whereas a zav and the like defile even in this case (see Hilchot Matmei Mishkav UMoshav 6:5; and see Chasdei David, Kuntres Torat HaOhel, par. 18).
as will be explained. The law of crushed impurity and the interposition of a tent is below 12:1 ff.
yerokah. Verdigris.
as will be explained in Hilchot Kelim. 1:3.
of wool that grew in the sea. It is a kind of sponge and resembles wool (Commentary on the Mishnah, Avot 5:14, Kelim 9:4; and see Hilchot Kil'ayim 10:1).
the substance of this tent does not receive impurity. Although hide and wool usually become impure by tent-impurity (above 5:12), these are pure because they originate in the sea.
although it brings the impurity etc.. For any tent with a handbreadth by a handbreadth that is a handbreadth above the ground brings the impurity to everything beneath it (below 12:1).
dung vessels. Vessels made of animal dung.
they do not receive impurity etc.. See also Hilchot Kelim 1:6.
and likewise a wooden vessel made to stay put. Because of its size it is meant to remain in its place and not be moved.
the chest and the migdal. Kinds of furniture meant for storage.
that hold forty se'ah of liquid. That can hold liquids in the amount of forty se'ah (about 285 liters).
base. Bottom.
they do not receive impurity at all etc.. See ibid. 3:1.
their flat ones. Vessels that have no receptacle.
pure. See also Hilchot Kelim 1:8.
and their receptacles. Vessels that have a receptacle.
and they become impure only from their airspace. Only when impurity enters them, even if it did not touch them (ibid. 13:1).
or by the shifting of a zav. A zav and his like defile people and pure vessels even by shifting alone, and even clay vessels (Hilchot Matmei Mishkav UMoshav 8:2).
and if it was encircled with a tight seal. It has a tight, secure cover.
as is explained in the Torah. Numbers 19:15, and see below 21:1.
golel. A cover placed over a corpse (above 2:15).
the skin of a fish and its bones. Its skin or its bones.
one who touches them. The same applies to one who spreads over them (see there and below, halakhah 6).
is impure with seven-day impurity for touching a golel. Since they are part of the grave, they defile one who touches them although they themselves are pure.
and likewise a jar. Made of clay.
whether standing or lying on its side. Whether the beam lies on the grave on its narrow side or its wide side (Kesef Mishneh).
and one who touches the end lying outside the grave is pure. Since the part extending outside the grave is not considered a golel.
he made its end a golel for the grave. He does not need the whole length of the beam for the golel, only its end.
and it stands over the grave like a tree. Set upright, with no part of it extending outside the grave.
of four by four handbreadths. Each of them is four handbreadths by four handbreadths, and together they cover the grave's cavity.
one who spreads over both of them is impure. For a golel defiles by tent (above 2:15).

pure, because the impurity has a way to go out through it. The size of an opening that keeps a sealed grave from defiling is four handbreadths (below 7:1), so once one stone is removed the other is no longer considered a golel (Arukh HaShulchan HaAtid 16:9-12).
the inner row. The row of stones closest to the grave.

a coffin that is hewn in the rock etc.. The corpse is buried in a cavity hewn in the rock (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 9:14; it is uncertain whether this is a rock detached from the ground and lying on it, or a rock attached to the ground).
one who touches the rock anywhere is pure. The rock is not considered part of the golel, and it does not defile as a grave because it is not sealed by a headstone but only by a golel.

and one who touches the golel is impure. One who touches the cover of the coffin (it seems that this passage presents the general principle, and the definition of which part of the coffin is considered the golel varies according to its shape as detailed in the following paragraphs; see Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.).
for only what is opposite its cavity is impure. And not the earth around the mouth of the pit, since that is ordinary ground and is not part of the golel.
and if he built a nefesh on top of it. He built a headstone on top of the coffin hewn in the rock.

this is like a sealed grave and defiles from all sides. The whole coffin defiles as a sealed grave does: one who spreads over it or touches it on any of its sides becomes impure (see above 2:15, below 7:1).
wide at the bottom and narrow at the top. The grave is hewn in the rock so that the sealed part of the coffin is at the bottom and its sides slope upward.
one who touches it from below. At the bottom of the coffin.
and from above. At the sides of the coffin.
the coffin was wide at the top and narrow at the bottom. The coffin was placed upside down so that its sealed part is at the top and its sides narrow downward.
one who touches it anywhere is impure. Since in this way the whole coffin is considered a golel for the corpse.
it was even. The sides of the coffin are parallel.
from the handbreadth next to its bottom and upward it is impure. This part of the rock is considered part of the coffin, which defiles as a golel.
from a handbreadth down it is pure. This is not considered part of the coffin (and see also above 1:11).

he bored a coffin in the rock and put the corpse inside it like a bolt. He laid the corpse horizontally, like a bolt of a lock passing from side to side (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 9:14; and see also Hilchot Mezuzah 5:8). Some explain that he dug a grave deep in the ground and put the corpse in standing, like the bolt of an upright door going from top to bottom (Arukh HaShulchan HaAtid, based on Bava Batra 101a; according to him Rambam retracted from his Commentary on the Mishnah).
except for the place of its opening. For the place of its opening is considered a golel.
when the courtyard is open to the air. That is, uncovered.
provided he does not touch the lintel of the cave. For one who touches the lintel of a corpse's tent becomes impure (above 1:11).

if it had four handbreadths... one who enters there is pure. A courtyard of this size is not considered part of the burial cave (and see Kesef Mishneh and Merkevet HaMishneh as to why, when the courtyard is covered, one who enters it does not become impure by tent).
a sealed house. One with no opening at all.
and breached its doorposts and sealed it. He removed its doorposts and then sealed it, thereby cancelling its status as an opening.
like a sealed grave. See above 2:15.
one who touches it from behind or from its roof is pure. For the house is no longer judged as a sealed grave.
and only what is opposite the opening is impure. One who touches the opening from outside, or who is beneath its space, becomes impure.
its opening is four handbreadths. An opening about 30 by 30 cm, since only through such an opening can a whole corpse be taken out.

all of them are impure. For the house defiles through its openings (as above, halakhah 1), because the corpse will eventually leave through one of the openings, and since we do not know which opening it will leave through, all are impure (Rabbi Shimshon and Rosh, Oholot 3:6).

and one sitting beside any of these openings under the ceiling... became impure. Although he sits outside the door of the house and does not touch it, he becomes impure by tent, since he sits beneath the lintel.
one of them was opened... it saved all the openings. Once we know through which opening the corpse will be taken out, the other openings no longer defile.
and the rest are pure because they are locked. If they were open they would be impure as part of the corpse's tent.
and the house is not like a sealed grave. Since it has openings, it does not defile from all its sides.
and likewise if he began to dig an opening. A new one in the wall.
from the time he begins to open. Even if he has not yet opened it to four by four.
if it had many windows and all of them were closed, all of them are pure. For the impurity is not normally taken out through a window.
if all were opened, they are impure. For they are considered part of the corpse's tent (see below 14:1).
one who spreads over both of them is impure. The large lintel that spreads over both openings is impure, and one beneath it becomes impure by tent.
the small one purified the large one. The small lintel is impure and the large one is pure.
if both were equal. The two openings are the same size side by side, and they have a single lintel spreading over both.
purified the other. The part of the lintel that spreads over the other opening is pure.
and he intended to take it out by the northern one. And now the northern one is impure and the southern one pure.
provided he does not scheme. That the brothers and relatives not scheme and say they will take it out by the southern one only in order to purify the northern one.
houses that open onto an akhsadra. A roofed open area in front of the houses, which opens onto the courtyard.
and the corpse is in one of them. And all the doorways of the house are locked (Kesef Mishneh).
the gatehouse. The entrance room of the house, facing the akhsadra (Kesef Mishneh explains that the gatehouse is the akhsadra itself).

the gatehouse and the houses are impure. Since the custom is to take the corpse out to the courtyard through the gatehouse that opens to the akhsadra and the houses, everything is impure (that is, where the doors of the other houses are open, so that the impurity enters through them; Kesef Mishneh).
and if not. If the custom is to take the corpse out of the house another way.

the gatehouse is impure and the houses are pure. Since it is in doubt whether the corpse will go out through the gatehouse, the akhsadra and the houses do not become impure, although with regard to the gatehouse itself the impurity goes out (see Merkevet HaMishneh; Sidrei Taharot, Oholot 114:2).
the inner room within the house is closed. An inner room inside the house, and the opening between it and the rest of the house is shut.
the outer house is pure. For the impurity does not go out through the opening to the rest of the house.
because the impurity returns and goes out through the window by which it entered. Therefore the house is pure, since otherwise windows would not protect the openings.
a space of a handbreadth by a handbreadth by a handbreadth in height. An empty space of a handbreadth by a handbreadth and a handbreadth high.
everything is impure, for everything is like a grave. This law applies to a built grave, but for wooden coffins the law is different (see below 12:6).
crushed. Compressed, without enough room.
one who touches opposite the impurity from above. If he touched the roof of the grave opposite the place of the impurity.
or one who spreads over it from above. Spreads above the place of the impurity without touching the roof of the grave.
for anything that defiles by tent from a corpse. Those listed above, 3:1.
a heap. A pile.
and vessels beside the impurity. Inside the heap or pile.
it is like a sealed grave. The entire heap or pile.
and defiles from all its sides. Therefore the vessels inside it are also impure.
he has nullified the house. It is no longer considered a tent that brings the impurity to what is inside it (see below 12:1).
and leaned a sukkah against the wall. The roof of the sukkah rests on the wall, so that it spreads over the crushed impurity beneath it (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 7:1).
the sukkah is impure. By the law of a corpse's tent.
a field in which a grave was lost. A corpse was buried in it and it is not known where.
its earth defiles by touch and by carrying, like a beit hapras. One who touches or carries a clod of its earth becomes impure, as with a beit hapras (above 2:16, below 10:2).
bones the size of a barleycorn. Which defile by touch and by carrying (ibid., halakhah 9).
aligned opposite the opening of a house. The opening of the upper room is aligned with the opening of the house and is not larger than it.
the upper room is pure. Since wherever the grave is, the upper room does not spread over it, because the tent of the house interposes between it and the impurity.
as will be explained. Below 12:1.

perhaps the threshold of the upper room is over the grave, and the upper room spreads over the grave. The grave may be beneath the wall of the house above which is the opening of the upper room, so that the lintel of the upper room's opening spreads over the grave.

it is permitted to sow any seed in it. Although with a beit hapras we fear that a bone the size of a barleycorn might be mixed with the seeds (below 10:8), in this field we do not fear that, since it is not known for certain that the grave was plowed over.
fruit trees. But non-fruit trees are permitted (Mishnah Oholot 18:3).

because the roots reach the corpse. In his Commentary on the Mishnah (Oholot 18:3) he wrote that the reason is that the fruits might become impure because of this (and Kesef Mishneh explains similarly). The commentators asked why the fruits become impure because of this (and see Merkevet HaMishneh, who writes that the concern is that the fruits will draw nourishment from the corpse, from which benefit is forbidden).
the mounds. Piles of earth.
these are presumed impure. Their earth is impure and one who spreads over them is impure (Tosefta Oholot 16:1).
because women bury stillborn infants there. And a nefel defiles like a complete corpse (above 2:1; and see also below 11:8).
and those afflicted with boils. Whose limbs fall off.
bury their limbs there. And a limb from a living person defiles like a complete corpse (above 2:3).

perhaps they were near a city that was destroyed or a road that was lost. It is possible that these mounds were once near a city or road adjacent to the cemetery, but the city and road no longer exist, and now they appear distant; therefore they are presumed impure.
for impurity was not established there. We do not know that there is a grave there.

one may not plant it or sow it, so as not to accustom people's feet to go there. Unlike a field in which a grave was lost, which may be sown (above, halakhah 3), and a beit hapras, which may be planted (below 10:8).
,. One who enters those becomes impure; in this field, since one who enters it is pure, they forbade sowing or planting it in order to reduce entry into it (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 18:4).

since it is near the cemetery, its owners have already despaired of it. Since this field is adjacent to the cemetery and is used by the public, it is no longer presumed to belong to its owners, and anyone may do with it as he wishes.
and ovens for sacred food are made from the earth of this place. One may make from it an oven in which to cook sacrificial foods, since the earth itself is presumed pure.
a grave that is found. A grave was found in a certain place and no one knew that a person was buried there.
it is permitted to remove it. Presumably it was buried in the field without the owner's permission.

its place is impure and forbidden for benefit until it is checked, as will be explained. The area around the grave is presumed impure out of concern that there are more graves there, and they forbade using it, as with a cemetery (see Hilchot Evel 14:13), until it is checked that no other dead are buried there, as explained in the next chapter (based on Kesef Mishneh).
and a known grave is forbidden to remove. Since the burial there was with the knowledge of the field's owner.
its place is pure and permitted for benefit. Since it is known, we do not worry that there are other graves here.
a grave that harms the public. For example, it is buried in a place where many people walk and they become impure because of it.

they remove it, and its place is impure and forbidden for benefit. This refers to the case of a grave that was found; but unlike an ordinary grave, which one may remove, a grave that harms the public must be removed (Chazon Ish, Oholot 22:20, based on Kesef Mishneh). It may also be explained that this refers even to a case where the grave was known, and nevertheless it may be removed for the public's sake. According to this explanation, some commentators say that the reason its place is impure and forbidden for benefit is a special decree so that people do not come to be lenient about removing graves (Even HaAzel, Hilchot Evel 14:20, subsection 10-11, which explains the previous halakhah similarly).
one who encounters a met mitzvah. A Jewish corpse lying on the road with no one to bury it (Hilchot Evel 3:8), whom every person is commanded to bury.
within the boundary. The boundary of the city (Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 5:3).
even within a saffron field. Which is an expensive spice, and burial in it would cause great loss.
he buys its place and he is buried where he was found. This is one of the enactments of Joshua son of Nun and his court (see ibid.).
he found it on the boundary. The border between two fields, where it is impossible to bury him.
he moves it to the sides. As explained below.
an uncultivated field. A field that has not been plowed.
on this side. Of the boundary.
a plowed field. A field that has been plowed.
a sown field. A field that has been sown.
he buries it in a vineyard field because of the tent of impurity. For a tree spreads more than a vineyard does.
it defiles retroactively. And all the pure things that were there in the past are impure.
even before twenty years. That this person is sure there was no grave here at a certain date, even if that date was more than twenty years ago.
it defiles only from the moment of its discovery onward. Since that place is presumed not to have had a grave, it is pure until the time a grave is found in it.
and on the intermediate days of a festival. For this is among the needs of the public that may be done on the intermediate days (see Hilchot Yom Tov 7:10-11).
exactly an olive's bulk. A precise quantity.
because in the end it will diminish in the ground. It will eventually shrink in the soil, and less than an olive's bulk of a corpse's flesh does not defile at all (above 3:15).
he dissolves. Dissolves the lime in water.
so as not to cause loss of the pure things. For if the marker did not extend a little past the sides, one might spread over the impurity.
so as not to cause loss of the Land of Israel. By increasing the area considered impure unnecessarily.
a field in which a grave was lost. On which the Sages decreed impurity because of the doubt.
and the overhanging branches and the projections. Trees or stones that cover the ground (see below 13:2), for example where there is doubt that impurity lies beneath them (Rashi, Mo'ed Katan 5b).
if it has no trees, it is known that a grave was lost in it. For in such a field it is forbidden to plant fruit trees (above, halakhah 3), and its law is that it defiles by tent (above, halakhah 1).

if it has trees, it is known that the grave was plowed up, as will be explained. Such a field (called a 'beit hapras') does not defile by tent (below 10:2) and it is permitted to plant trees in it (ibid., halakhah 8; and see further ibid., halakhah 10).
if there is lime between them. On the ground between them.
for this is only a building. It is reasonable that the potsherd was part of a building, and this lime is from the building.
and the lime was smeared on their tops on this side and that. They poured lime on their tops and it spread to all sides.
if he found its four boundaries marked, they are pure. Since all the field's boundaries are marked, we assume the marking refers to the field between them.
for one does not distance the marker from the place of the impurity. Therefore we assume the entire field is impure and not only a certain area within it.
or found people who were slain. Even if they are not in one pit.
he does not worry that perhaps this place was a cemetery. Since it is not customary to bury in these ways, there is no concern that there are other graves there (as explained below, halakhah 3).
the loose earth beneath it. The moist earth next to the corpse, which is presumed soft because it contains some of its blood and fluid.

and he digs three fingerbreadths into virgin soil and removes it all. He digs into the hard ground beneath the corpse to a depth of three fingerbreadths (about 6 cm), since up to this depth we must be concerned that it absorbed some of the blood and the dissolved flesh of the corpse (Commentary on the Mishnah, Nazir 9:3).

tevusat hamet. From the term for the blood of the corpse that is soaked and absorbed in the earth (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 16:3; some read 'tefusat hamet', explaining that the corpse takes hold of and acquires its place, and therefore a small amount of earth must be taken with it when it is removed; see Nazir 65a and the commentators there).
he gathers all the bones in it and it is pure. For those who were slain have no tevusah (below, halakhah 3).

and likewise one who removes his grave from his field etc.. For example, they buried him there with the intention of removing him after some time, and therefore he has no tevusah (Arukh HaShulchan HaAtid 21:9).

for they are like two caves and the courtyard between them. For their practice was to bury in caves, each cave being six cubits long and the courtyard between them six cubits long, and for added certainty two more cubits are added (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 16:3).
even though they are a neighborhood of graves. Even though the three dead that he found are a neighborhood of graves.
for there is a basis for the matter. Since a corpse was found at the end of twenty cubits, there is a basis to think there is a cemetery here, and one must continue checking.
one who was slain. Buried where he was killed, for it is reasonable that he was buried there temporarily.
or sitting or lying not in the usual way. For it is not the way of Israel to be buried like this.
for their presumption is that they are gentiles. Only gentiles bury in this manner, and gentiles do not have the law of a neighborhood of graves, as explained in the next halakhah.
and its tevusah. The earth beneath the corpse, as explained above, halakhah 1.

if there is between one and another from four cubits to eight, enough for a bier and its bearers etc.. Between graves one generally assumes a free area of this size, used by those burying the dead at the time of burial.
he must worry that perhaps this is a cemetery. And now the field is presumed impure until it is checked that there are no more graves in it.

they have no grave impurity. They do not have the law of a neighborhood of graves (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 16:3). And one who walks there need not worry about tent-impurity (see also Hilchot Evel 3:3).
since they do not defile by tent. As above 1:13.
one who touches their grave is pure. For grave impurity depends on tent-impurity (see above 7:4), so even if more gentiles are buried there, they do not defile one who walks there.
until he touches the bone of impurity or carries it. For the dead of gentiles defile by touch and carrying (above 1:12).
for if it were removed from a living person he would die. A person cannot live without this limb.
and corpses found exposed on the surface of the field etc.. Even though they were not slain, since they are not buried they have no tevusah and no neighborhood of graves.
and it has no neighborhood of graves. Since it was buried without permission, there is no concern that there are other graves there.
or found three kukhin, or a kukh, a nekiya and a cave. He found different kinds of excavations made for burial, although he did not find the dead themselves.
and one was known. It was known that a corpse was buried there.
until he reaches rock or virgin soil, which is ground that appears not to have been worked. Then there is no concern that there is a grave beneath.
and found a potsherd, it is as at the beginning. The discovery of the potsherd proves that this ground was worked, and there is still concern for a grave beneath it.
he need not dig one continuous furrow. Without interruption.
for between one grave and another there is no less than a cubit. For the practice with burial caves is that the spaces between them are greater than a cubit (see Hilchot Mekhirah 21:6).
or a puddle. A water channel (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 16:6).
for the neighborhood of graves was interrupted. For it is not the practice to bury in any of these.
one who takes out this earth from the examination is pure. As long as we do not know for certain that there is impurity there, this earth does not defile.
eats terumah. If he is a kohen.
and one who clears the pile. One who removes the stones of a collapse in order to rescue the people beneath it.
for he knows for certain that the dead are there under the pile. Therefore he is impure and forbidden terumah.
an impure pile. A pile of stones with impurity beneath it.
and the other two are impure. Due to doubt.
all of them are presumed impure. There is concern that the examiner did not examine well, and all are impure due to doubt.
and all three will be pure. Since a thorough examination was made and the impurity was not found, it is reasonable that it is no longer there.
one who spreads over it is impure by Torah law. For a nefel defiles by tent (above 2:1).
even though a weasel and a polecat are found there. And it is possible that they dragged the nefalim out of the pit (see below 11:9).
as we explained in Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah. 18:17.
and in several places. See Hilchot Kil'ayim 10:27; Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 16:1.
as we explained in Hilchot Shegagot. In chapter 8.
were ground fine. Were pulverized.
and were scattered. Were dispersed.
even if he plowed over the coffin. The burial coffin; in this case the plow did not reach the corpse's bones at all.
with slabs. Marble slabs.
and even if there were two stories' height over the coffin. The coffin was buried in the ground to a depth of two stories.
the entire square that is a beit arba'at se'in. A beit se'ah is an area of fifty by fifty cubits.
as we explained. Above 2:16.
or struck it against a rock or a fence. He struck the plow against them and thereby shook off the earth from it.
for it did not reach him in the course of the plowing. It did not drag along anything that might have stuck to the plow before he shook the earth off it.
and the presumption of exposed bones is that they are an animal's. And they do not defile, and one who plows them does not create a beit hapras.

or plowed a field in which a grave was lost etc.. In that case it is not certain that the grave was plowed up (and although this field already defiles by touch, carrying and tent as above 8:1, it does not become a beit hapras with respect to the prohibition of sowing it and the like; see ibid., halakhah 3).
for a person cannot forbid something that is not his. For this principle see also Hilchot Avodah Zarah 8:1; Hilchot Kil'ayim 5:8 and elsewhere.
a sharecropper. A person who receives a field to work in return for a certain percentage of the crop.

an apitropos. A person appointed to be in charge of property. [Note: the vocalization of this word follows the Greek original. In Rambam's autograph Commentary on the Mishnah several forms of vocalizing this word appear: sometimes the first pe is vocalized with a kubutz, sometimes with a patach (and in some places the pe is not vocalized).]
he plowed a grave in his field and his neighbor's field together. He continued the plowing into his neighbor's field.
for there is no beit hapras for gentiles. Likewise there is no beit hapras outside the Land of Israel (below 11:11).
a beit hapras field above. Higher up the mountain.
even if it was red and they whitened it. The earth of the pure field was red and became white from beit hapras earth washed into it.
and they decreed impurity only on a clod in its natural form. Therefore even the earth that washed down no longer defiles, since it is not in its natural form (and see also below 11:3, 15:5).
because the roots go down etc.. In this way the roots do not reach the corpse's bones (see above 8:3 and the explanation there).
and below three. Handbreadths (see below, halakhah 12).
only seed that is harvested. For example grain. But not vegetables and the like, which, when uprooted from the ground, bring up with them some beit hapras earth.
and if he sowed and uprooted. From the root, a plant that is normally harvested (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 18:2).
he stores his grain in it. He stockpiles the grain in the beit hapras itself and does not take it out of there.
and he sifts the grain in two sieves. He sifts the grain twice.
and legumes in three sieves. For with legumes the earth sticks more.
the etzah. The straw of legumes.
even if it is a beit arba'at korin. For example, where many graves were plowed there, since a single grave creates only a beit arba'at se'in (above, halakhah 2; Rabbi Shimshon, Oholot 17:3).

and even if it is drawn from a place of soft mud etc.. The soil of the field is soft mire; although this soil cannot be plowed and does not become a beit hapras, perhaps the grave was plowed when the soil there was ordinary (Arukh HaShulchan HaAtid 22:19).
and even if pure fields surround it on its four sides. That is, the fields around it were examined and declared pure (Rabbi Shimshon, Oholot, ibid.).
he found a marked field. It was marked initially because of the grave in it (see above 8:9), and afterward the grave was lost or plowed up.
as we explained. Above 8:10.
provided there is in that place an elder or a Torah scholar. That the planting of the tree in this field was done on his instruction.
on a person or an animal whose strength is good, it is pure. Even if they shift the impurity, it is not considered that the rider shifts it.
even if he was careful and did not shake, it is impure etc.. Since they are not stable, they are considered part of the beit hapras earth.
his knees. His knees.
until it drops dung. From great effort.
he gathers all the earth that can be shifted. The earth that can move from its place when one walks on it.
and dissolves. He will sift it thoroughly (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 18:4).
and removes every bone the size of a barleycorn found there, and he becomes pure. After the sifting, the field's earth no longer defiles and he may leave it in place.
and likewise if he hoed it. Dug up the field.
and examined at the time of hoeing only on the surface. And did not bother to examine in depth.
the land of the nations. Any land that is not the Land of Israel.

at first they decreed only on its clod. On a clod of its earth (see below, halakhah 3). The reason for the decree is that they treat the dead lightly and bury them anywhere (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 2:3; above 2:16).
and most of it. Most of his body.
and likewise a clay vessel. Which receives impurity through its airspace.

and other vessels, most of which he brought in etc.. Since they do not receive impurity through their airspace, their law is the same as that of a person (and see also Hilchot Tumat Tzara'at 16:6; Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 6:6).
for because of the impurity of its earth, terumah and sacrificial foods are burned. See also Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 13:13.
and he needs sprinkling on the third and the seventh. With the ashes of the red heifer, like any person impure through a corpse.
but only immersion and nightfall. He need only immerse and wait for evening to become pure.
they suspend. They leave it undecided.
as we explained. Above 2:16.
like the seal of the marzefin. A seal of clay with which large sacks used for storing goods are sealed.
and it is like a large bundle of sacks. A bundle of threads used for sewing sacks, which are thicker than ordinary threads.
that came with vegetables. Whose earth stuck to vegetables that were uprooted from it.
in its natural form. In its entirety.
and there were a se'ah or two se'ah of seals. The letters were sealed with clay made from the impure earth of outside the Land, and there were many seals.
before they were fired, they are impure because of the land of the nations. As long as the clay has not been fired it has the law of earth.
as we explained. Above 5:6.
impure with seven-day impurity. Even though it is not customary to bury in these places.
and in a place where the sea rises in its fury. When there is a high tide.
pure from the impurity of touching the land of the nations. For in these places it is certainly impossible to bury.

in a shidah, a chest and a migdal that fly in the air, he is impure. Even though the furniture is suspended in the air and the person inside does not touch the ground and is not exposed to the air of the land of the nations.
for a thrown tent is not called a tent. A tent that is moved from place to place is not considered a tent for interposing against impurity (see below 13:5).

Syria. The lands that David conquered outside the land of Canaan; their status is greater than that of outside the Land but not at the level of the Land of Israel (Hilchot Terumot 1:3; for the details of its borders see ibid. 1:9).

therefore if it was adjacent to the Land of Israel... one can enter it in purity in a shidah, chest and migdal. Since its airspace is pure, it is possible to leave the Land of Israel and enter its airspace without becoming impure when there is no impurity in between.
it is examined and is pure. Since it is adjacent to the Land of Israel, it is possible to enter it without becoming impure, after examining it.
it defiles like the land of the nations. Its earth and airspace are impure.
until it is examined. As below, halakhah 9.
perhaps they buried stillborn infants in it. Although gentiles do not defile by tent (above 1:13), there is concern for impurity by touch or carrying (see Responsa of Rambam 145).
a dwelling of the nations. A place where gentiles lived.
and how long may he stay. The gentile.
and she aborts a nefel that defiles. Until it is forty days old its form is not complete and it does not defile (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 10:1).
even a slave or a woman. With no other woman or man with them (see Merkevet HaMishneh; Tiferet Yisrael, Oholot 18:7).
a saris. One with a physical defect that prevents him from fathering children.
a boy nine years and one day old. From this age on his relations are considered relations (see Hilchot Ishut 11:3).
a slave of an Israelite. A slave belonging to a Jew; if he were a gentile's slave, he himself would make a dwelling of the nations, as above.
or a boy of nine. Who knows how to ensure that a nefel is not buried there (Kesef Mishneh).
the deep drains. The sewer channels beneath the house.
and the foul water. Collected in the courtyard; in these places gentiles throw their stillborn infants.
the colonnades. Rows of columns covered by a roof.
and the burganin. Towers made for storing fruit (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 18:10); some explain that it means the huts of the fruit watchmen (Rabbenu Ovadiah of Bertinoro, ibid.).
and the gatehouse. The entrance room of the house or courtyard.
and the airspace of a courtyard. A courtyard that is not roofed.
and the place of the legions. Military camps. All of these are temporary dwellings in which people do not live permanently.
a courtyard that is impure because of a dwelling of the nations. Because gentiles live in a roofed place within it.
and its airspace. The open area of the courtyard.
and its neighbors. The cities around it.
even though they are exempt from tithes and from the seventh year. For these purposes they are considered outside the Land (see Hilchot Terumot 1:5, 1:9).
and the presumption of the roads of those who came up from Babylonia. Roads by which those who came up from Babylonia held the right to ascend to the Land.
a handbreadth by a handbreadth square and a handbreadth high. A cover of a handbreadth by a handbreadth and a handbreadth in height.
brings the impurity and interposes against the impurity. As explained below.
an olive's bulk of a corpse. And likewise anything that defiles by tent.
placed in the open air. In a place that is not roofed.
and tzinorot. Like small forks or metal pieces bent at the end like a hook, used for spinning and the like.
this brings the impurity to the vessels and they are impure. For everything that is with the impurity under one tent becomes impure (above 1:10).
everything opposite the impurity is impure because they spread over the impurity etc.. And everything that spreads over the impurity becomes impure (above 1:10).
for anything less than a handbreadth in height is considered as touching. As if there were no tent at all.
and impurity beneath it is crushed impurity. And it breaks through upward and breaks through downward.
as we explained. Above 7:5.
whether the tent's posts were. That the tent rests on them.
even if they were vessels that do not receive impurity at all. For example vessels made of dung, stones or earth.
a board that was placed etc.. For example, the board is not a vessel and by itself interposes against impurity.
four spits or four reeds. Which are vessels that receive impurity.

even not opposite the impurity they are impure. The board does not interpose against the impurity since it rests on a person or vessels; therefore, just as everything beneath it is impure (for it is a tent), so everything above it becomes impure, even if it is not aligned with the impurity.

and if there was impurity on the board and vessels beneath it, all the vessels beneath the board are impure. The impurity lying on the board descends beneath it, and since the board now spreads over the impurity, it extends beneath all of it and defiles everything beneath.
stones. That are not vessels.

and dung vessels, stone vessels, earthen vessels that come in measure. Those that are stationary and large (for the definition of this term see above 6:2). The same applies to a wooden vessel that comes in measure (as is evident below 13:3, Kesef Mishneh).
a board. That interposes against impurity.
a new oven. In which a fire has never been lit.
and it extends beyond it on all its sides by a handbreadth. The board projects around the oven on all sides by a handbreadth by a handbreadth.
because a new oven is not like vessels for this purpose. Therefore the board interposes against the impurity, since it does not rest on a vessel (and see also below 21:8).

and it extends beyond this oven and beyond that oven. The board projects outside the ovens at the two ends only but does not extend beyond their sides (similar to the law of a single oven in the next paragraph; Riko, Kiryat Sefer and others).
for they are like two tents side by side. And impurity does not pass from one tent to another (see below 16:7).
a mardea. A stick used to strike and direct oxen (an ox goad).
if its circumference was a handbreadth. The circumference measure of an average ox goad (see below 22:4).
even though its width is only a finger and a third. Which is about a third of a handbreadth.
and to any other person. Who is not carrying the goad.
are not like a grave. They do not defile from all around by touch and tent as a grave does (see above 2:15, 7:4).

if there is between the coffin's cover and the corpse a height of a handbreadth, it interposes. The coffin is considered a wooden vessel that comes in measure, which has the law of a tent that interposes against impurity when it has a handbreadth of height (see above, halakhah 2; Mikdash David, Taharot 49:3).
since in some there is no handbreadth of space there. In coffins of this kind the coffin does not interpose and the impurity breaks upward ('crushed impurity').
because part of it is part of a tent. That part which does not have the measure of a handbreadth is considered part of the tent, and the rest of the tent has the measure of a handbreadth.
as we explained. Above 7:4-5.
when it is round, three handbreadths. For any object with a circumference of three handbreadths has a width of a handbreadth (below, halakhah 8).
a se'ah. A round, hollow vessel.
that is lying on its side in the open air. Lying on the ground with no tent above it.

so that the height of the upper side is a handbreadth and a half etc.. Only if the se'ah's diameter is close to a handbreadth and a half (which is a third of four and a half handbreadths) will the se'ah's cavity have the measure of a tent (a handbreadth by a handbreadth) at a handbreadth's height from the ground.

therefore if it was raised above the ground by half a handbreadth and its circumference was three etc.. The half-handbreadth beneath the se'ah combines with the half-handbreadth inside it so that there is the measure of a tent in the se'ah's cavity even when its circumference is only three handbreadths.
and likewise a round pillar. That is not hollow.
and lying on the ground. Lying down.
it does not bring the impurity beneath its side. For example, the impurity lies on the ground beneath the rounded slope of the pillar and pure things lie beside it.
until its circumference is twenty-four handbreadths. As explained below.

impurity breaks upward and breaks downward. The pillar does not bring the impurity beneath its side since there is no measure of a tent there, and therefore the impurity defiles only what is opposite it.
on the fundamentals that the Sages rely on in the calculation of all laws. The calculation here is based on mathematical principles on which the Sages rely in many halakhot.
and any handbreadth by handbreadth square has a diagonal of a handbreadth and two fifths. See also Hilchot Shabbat 12:18.
as we explained. Above 12:1.
or a hole that water or creeping things dug etc.. In the ground or in a wall and the like.
or that a salt-bug ate. Created by a melachat (a type of creature) that ate through it and made a hole.
this is a tent and it brings. The impurity to everything inside the tent's space.
and interposes. Against the impurity, so that it does not pass to the other side of the tent (see above 12:1).
the branches of trees. Boughs.
if they can bear a medium plastering and they stand. If they can bear a layer of ceiling that is neither too heavy nor too light without falling.
these bring and interpose by Torah law. For they are considered a strong, sound tent.
that come in measure. That are stationary and large (for the definition of this term see above 6:2) and are not considered vessels but tents (above 12:2).
and flat hide vessels. Sheets made of hide.
and a mat and a reed mat. Usually woven from various kinds of reeds.
for they are made as tents. They have a slope or walls beneath them; otherwise they are treated as vessels and do not interpose (below, halakhah 4).

provided that the head of this one is between the feet of that one and all of them are stuck together. That there are no gaps between them; then they are all considered one tent for bringing impurity.
and a bird that has settled. Sitting in one place (but if it flutters in the air it neither brings nor interposes; below, halakhah 5).
and one who burrows in the ears of grain etc.. Digs and makes a tent within a heap of grain.

and foods that have not been rendered susceptible so that they do not become impure. That have not been rendered susceptible to impurity (see Hilchot Tumat Ochlin 1:1-2); if they have been rendered susceptible they do not interpose, even if they did not actually become impure (below, halakhah 4).
they are like trees and bring and interpose. Unlike other seeds and vegetables attached to the ground (below, halakhah 5).
iris. Mint (Rabbi Y. Kafih).
and ivy. A climbing plant.
and donkey greens. A plant not eaten by people (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 8:1).
and likewise the overhanging branches and the projections. When they can bear a medium plastering (above, halakhah 2).
and the ledges and the cornices. Structures projecting from the wall.
and the shekifin. Projections coming out of rocks.
and the gechirim. Curved walls (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 8:2).
and the shananim. Teeth of rock.
or rendered susceptible. That were rendered susceptible to impurity even though they did not become impure.
and a hand mill. Small grinding stones for grinding by hand.
for it is included among stone vessels. Which, although they do not receive impurity, do not interpose (above 12:1).
except for the four vegetables that we enumerated. Above, halakhah 3.
and a canopy of hail, snow, frost, ice and salt. A cover made of them, for a tent made of all of these melts quickly and does not last.
and one who skips from place to place. Hops on one foot over the impurity.
and one who leaps. On both feet (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 8:5).
