and a cloak that flutters. The wind lifts the cloak and it does not rest in place.
with something that can hold it. So that it does not move from its place.
for we already explained. Above, halakhah 5.
the stretched warp. The threads stretched in the loom.
and the bed cords. The ropes stretched between the beams of the bed, on which the mattress is laid.
and the baskets. Baskets made of netting.
and the lattices in the windows. Nets placed in windows.
in the holes of the baskets. In the openings in these baskets.
as will be explained. Below 14:1, 14:4.
for use. For the purpose of using it (see below, halakhah 7).
its measure is like a pundion. The size of a coin called a pundion, which is less than a handbreadth (and see below, halakhah 3).
and leaned against this window. From outside, so that the window's lintel spreads over it.
and a window made for light has no ceiling over it etc.. For if there is a ceiling over it, it darkens it, and it is not considered a window for light (see below, halakhah 5).
that a salt-bug ate. See above 13:1.

its measure is a full fist, which is like the large head of a person. 'Fist' means a roof tile from the tiles of the roof, and here a tile the size of a large person's head is meant (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 17:12; and see also Rashbam, Exodus 21:18). Some explain that agrof is a clenched hand (as the word means today), and according to this view it refers to the fist of a well-known man in their days who was fleshy ('ben beteach', Mishnah Kelim, ibid.), so that his fist was the size of a person's head (Rashi, Bekhorot 37b; and see Ramban, Exodus, ibid.).
for thought here is like action. Although for other purposes thought is not like action (see Hilchot Kelim 8:10).

the height of two fingers by the width of the thumb. About 4 by 2 cm, which is a measure smaller than a handbreadth but larger than a pundion (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 13:1; and see Piskei VeShitot).
a lattice. A net.
if there is in one place of it etc.. If one of its openings has the measure for taking out impurity (and see also above 13:8).
and rafafot. Nets made of wood.
exposed to the air. Open to a place that is not roofed.
as we said. Above, halakhah 1.
its measure is a handbreadth wide. For now it does not serve for light but for use.
he put the ceiling in the middle of the window. The house he built is lower than the first house, so its ceiling reaches the middle of the window.
or the carpenter left in it an open place above or below. The carpenter built the door so that it does not cover the entire space of the doorway.
or he closed the door and did not fully seal it. He did not close the door all the way.
and air remained between the two doors. In a door made of two parts. Likewise if a gap remained between the door and the doorpost (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 13:3).
if the opening was like a fist. Since these openings were not made deliberately or were not made for use, their measure is a fist.
a window for use. A window made for use, through which the impurity enters and leaves with a handbreadth opening (above 14:1).
if with something that interposes against the impurity. That is, something that does not receive impurity (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 6:2).
provided it is something that he does not intend to remove. Only in such a case is the window considered blocked.
with foods that have not been rendered susceptible. That have not been rendered susceptible to impurity (see Hilchot Tumat Ochlin 1:1-2).
if they were rotten. Not fit to eat.
rotten straw. Not fit for any use.
grain that grew. Next to the wall.
lest it damage the wall. By its roots (and see also Hilchot Shekhenim 9:2).
its root. Its root.
a jar. Of clay (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 6:2).
dried figs. Dried figs.
and the mouth of the jar faces the impurity. In this way the impurity enters it; for if the back of the jar faces the impurity it does not become impure and it interposes (below, halakhah 4).
for the jar is impure. It became impure by the impurity in the house, and therefore it does not itself interpose.
a basket. A large basket.
and rags that are not three by three. Rags smaller than three by three fingerbreadths (about 6 by 6 cm), for smaller than this measure they do not receive impurity (Hilchot Kelim 22:21).
and the limb and flesh hanging on an impure animal etc.. Which do not receive impurity (see Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 2:5; Hilchot Tumat Ochlin 2:6), and are not fit for anything.
and an impure bird. That is not kosher to eat.
and a bound gentile etc.. For gentiles do not receive impurity by Torah law (above 1:13).
for no one can untie him. Out of fear of the government.
and an eight-month baby. Born after eight months of pregnancy, who does not receive impurity (ibid., halakhah 14).
for it is forbidden to move him. He is like a stone that has no use (see Hilchot Shabbat 25:6).
and not for tanning. For the purpose of tanning hides.
and likewise a worn-out Torah scroll. Which requires burial (Hilchot Sefer Torah 10:3).
if he decided etc.. That he decided to bury it there and does not intend to remove it.
for they are fit. For use, and he intends to remove them from there.
and receive impurity. See Hilchot Tumat Ochlin 1:22.

and likewise less than an egg's bulk of foods that have not been rendered susceptible are not important to him and he does not intend to remove them. For if they were in a larger quantity they would be important to him and he would intend to remove them, and if they have been rendered susceptible they are able to receive impurity and do not interpose.
in less than an olive's bulk etc.. At these measures, none of those listed here receive impurity (above 3:15; Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 4:13).
because it does not become impure from its back. As explained above 6:3.
even to let blood with it. A repulsive vessel can be used for bloodletting, but when it is perforated it cannot be used at all.
a quarter of bones. The measure of a quarter-kav of bones that defiles by tent (above 2:9).
and the like of the bones that defile by tent. For their details see above, ibid., halakhah 8.

for the bone combines with the bones. Although the bone in the window does not have the measure of impurity, it does not interpose since it combines with the other bones through the tent (see above 4:8).
but a bone smaller than a barleycorn is diminished by an olive's bulk of flesh etc.. These things do not combine (ibid., halakhah 3).

in afflicted warp and woof. Warp and woof threads of wool or linen that became impure through leprosy (and they defile immediately when spun, Hilchot Tumat Tzara'at 13:8; but with other impurities they do not receive impurity as long as they have not been woven into a garment, Hilchot Kelim 1:11-12).
with a clod from a beit hapras. Above 10:1.
for they said only a clod in its natural form. Above 10:7, 11:3; and since he made a brick out of it, it is not in its natural form.
if it had substance etc.. Sometimes the cobwebs are thick and sometimes thin (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 13:5).
an aruvah. An opening in the ceiling.
whether it has a handbreadth opening. Which is the measure through which the impurity leaves the tent (above 14:1).
for it is exposed to the air. Since the opening is open to the sky and nothing spreads over it, the impurity does not pass from the house to what is beneath the opening.
the entire house is impure. For even if only part of the impurity is inside the house, the house becomes impure (see above 4:9).

and opposite the entire aruvah is impure. According to several commentators there is an error here and it should be emended to: 'and opposite the impurity is impure', meaning that only one who spreads opposite the impurity becomes impure, but the rest of the space of the aruvah is pure since there is no tent there (Ra'avad, based on Mishnah Oholot 10:1, and see Kesef Mishneh); but some retain the version before us (see Kiryat Sefer, Merkevet HaMishneh and Mayim Tehorim, Oholot 10:1, note 4).
like the measure. That defiles by tent.

and if not, the house is impure and opposite the aruvah is pure. When the aruvah does not have a handbreadth opening, one who spreads does not become impure unless there is the measure that defiles; the reason is explained by the commentators on the Mishnah (Rosh, Tiferet Yisrael and Acharon Rishon, Oholot 10:3).
everything is impure, and the person who mixed in the impurity is impure because he became a tent over the impurity. For the person brings the impurity and does not interpose against it (above 12:2).

for he spread over the impurity. Since the impurity came first, the person spreads over it when he places his foot over the aruvah (and although no impurity goes out of the house when the aruvah lacks a handbreadth opening, nevertheless when the impurity lies directly beneath the opening it defiles one who spreads opposite it even if the opening lacks a handbreadth; Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 10:2).
for his foot is part of the tent etc.. Since the person's foot plugged the aruvah, it is considered part of the ceiling and does not receive impurity (ibid.).
until an olive's bulk was found in the airspace of the aruvah. A raven brought the olive's bulk into the aruvah and the aruvah's mouth was blocked (Sidrei Taharot, Oholot 149:1).

even though it does not have a handbreadth opening, the house is impure. The impurity joins the house's ceiling and defiles everything inside it (ibid.; and see Kesef Mishneh, who explained otherwise).
and impurity in the house opposite the aruvot is pure etc.. Like the law of an aruvah in a house without an upper room (above, halakhah 1).
and placed something that receives impurity etc.. And thereby everything became one tent.
everything is impure. The house, the upper room and between the aruvot (see Piskei VeShitot).
for an impure thing does not interpose. As explained above 13:4.
whether above or below. Whether on the aruvah of the house or the aruvah of the upper room.

the house and the upper room are impure, for he mixed in the impurity. Since the cover receives impurity and spreads opposite it, it mixes the impurity into the whole house and the upper room (for the reason, see Maharam, Oholot 10:4; and specifically when the impurity preceded it, Rosh, Oholot 10:5, and as above, halakhah 1).
only the house is impure. And even when the cover is on the aruvah of the upper room, the impurity does not pass to the upper room since the opening lacks a handbreadth (see Maharam, ibid.).
as we explained. Above 14:2.
one who makes a hole in the plastering. Makes a hole in the floor of the upper room.
the leg of a bed. One of the legs of the bed, which receives impurity.
and the leg of the bed was plugging the aruvah. In a way that it is visible in the ceiling of the house (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 12:4).

if it does not have a handbreadth opening, the upper room is pure. For the impurity does not go out into the upper room through less than a handbreadth opening (and this is where the impurity is not opposite the leg; see Tosafot Yom Tov, Oholot 12:4, in the name of Maharam).
and the leg of the bed is impure like vessels that spread. For the leg is visible inside the house.
its measure is a full fist, as we explained. Above 14:2.
and a pot. Made of clay.
so that if it were lifted it would come out snugly from the aruvah. With no gap between the ceiling and the pot.
crushed between it and the ground. It has no space of a handbreadth (above 7:5).
and the entire house is pure. Since there is no tent that brings the impurity to the house.
for it is a tent. The handbreadth beneath the pot with the rest of the house is considered one tent, since there is no gap between them.

but the inside of the pot and its back are pure, for a clay vessel does not become impure from its back. Although even vessels that do not receive impurity do not interpose against it (as above 12:1), apparently this does not apply to the back of a clay vessel (and see Rabbi Shimshon and Rosh, Oholot 10:6, who gave another reason).
and the airspace of the pot is exposed to the air. The house does not spread over it, and therefore it is pure even though the rest of the house is impure.

the entire house is pure. And the inside of the pot and its back are impure (as for what is beneath the pot, in the Commentary on the Mishnah he wrote that it is pure, but Chasdei David, Oholot 11:5, inferred from Rambam's wording here that it is impure; nevertheless the impurity does not pass from there to the rest of the house).

a handbreadth opening was found between it and the edges of the aruvah... the house is pure. The impurity does not pass from beneath the pot into the house when there is a gap between them, and specifically when it has the measure of a handbreadth opening (for the reason see Merkevet HaMishneh; Chasdei David, Oholot, ibid.).
placed beside the threshold of the house. Outside the threshold at the entrance of the house.
a handbreadth of it is found within the lintel. The lintel is slightly longer than the threshold, so that a handbreadth of the pot lies beneath it.
impurity breaks upward and breaks downward. For example, the impurity is in a part that is not beneath the lintel and has no tent above it (Kesef Mishneh).

and its inside and back are pure. The impurity does not enter it from the house since it is not inside the tent. The commentators explain that this is where the pot's wall is beneath the lintel while its mouth is outside the lintel, so the impurity does not enter it (Rabbi Shimshon and Rosh, Oholot 10:7; Ra'avad; and see Kesef Mishneh on Rambam's view).

if the impurity was inside it or on its back, the house is impure etc.. The impurity descends beneath the pot and from there enters the house (Rabbi Shimshon, ibid.; and see Chazon Ish, Oholot 14:10, who found it difficult that it says here that the impurity goes out from the house to beneath the pot and suggested emending the wording, but in the Commentary on the Mishnah he explained as written here, that the impurity first enters the house and from there goes out beneath the pot, and the reason requires further study).

therefore if it did not touch the lintel with a handbreadth... the house is pure. Since the pot is outside the house, as long as it does not touch the lintel at a handbreadth it is not considered one tent with the house.
the beams of the house and the upper room that have no plastering on them. The house and upper room are roofed with beams only and there are gaps between the beams.
and they are aligned beam opposite beam and space opposite space. The beams are parallel to each other.
and between them is a space of a handbreadth. Between one beam and its neighbor.
beneath all of them is impure. Since the beams of the upper room are aligned with the space between the house's beams so that there is no gap between them, everything is considered one tent.
a house whose roof and walls cracked. Along the entire length.
the vessels in its inner half are pure. The impurity does not pass from the outer half to the inner half since there is a gap between the two parts.

and if it was less than this, they are impure. Although there is still a gap between the two halves, since the impurity's way is to go out (and the opening is in the outer half) and the gap is very narrow, it passes to the outer half.
an akhsadra that cracked. A roofed open area whose ceiling cracked along its entire length.
for it is two tents side by side. There is no inner and outer here, and therefore the impurity does not pass from one to the other.
he mixed in the impurity. As above, halakhah 1.

until there is a handbreadth of height beneath the crack. That there be something spreading over the ground at a handbreadth's height parallel to the crack (as above, halakhah 5, regarding a pot beneath an aruvah).
for a person is hollow etc.. See also below 18:2.
and the upper side. Of this person lying on the ground.
vessels. Clothes.
mixes in the impurity. For the upper garment is considered a tent a handbreadth above the ground (and see further below 17, end of halakhah 4).
a projection that comes out of the doorway of the house and faces downward. A protrusion extending from the doorpost and projecting outward, with its edge bent downward.
twelve handbreadths. About a meter.
this brings the impurity. If there is impurity in the house, what is beneath it is impure, and vice versa.
in any amount. Even though it does not have a handbreadth opening, since it is considered part of the doorway.
in a sound tent of a handbreadth. A tent of a handbreadth by a handbreadth by a handbreadth that is not flimsy, which brings the impurity by Torah law (above 13:1-2).
the crowns and apples that come out of the building. Projecting ornaments made on a building for decoration.
and even if there was a reed beside the lintel the width of the doorway. It looks as if it extends the doorway.
surrounds the whole house. On the outside (and has a handbreadth width).
and eats a handbreadth of the doorway. Enters a little above the doorway by a handbreadth.
brings the impurity. If there is impurity beneath it, the impurity enters the house through the part projecting over the doorway.

and impurity in the house, vessels beneath it are impure. Although the projection does not eat a handbreadth of the doorway, the impurity goes out through it and the vessels beneath it become impure. As for the reason, some explained that it is because the impurity's way is to go out (Rabbi Shimshon; Responsa of Rivash, no. 394).
and likewise in a courtyard surrounded by an akhsadra. Where the akhsadra's roof extends slightly into the doorway of the house in the courtyard.
that is made for use. Whose measure for taking the impurity out and in is a handbreadth opening (above 14:1).
even if it was the width of a thumb. Which is a quarter of the measure of a handbreadth.
brings the impurity. Even though it does not have a handbreadth opening, since it is considered part of the window.
the height of two fingers. About 4 cm.
that is made for light. Whose measure is like a pundion (above, ibid.).
and even a height of any amount. Without limit.
a structure projecting in front of the window. A windowsill.
does not bring the impurity. For it is beneath the window.
if it had a projection. In the window.

we regard the structure as if it were not there etc.. Since the sill was made to lean on and not for the purpose of any tent, we regard it as if it were not there and it does not interpose between the impurity and the projection (Merkevet HaMishneh).
two projections etc.. Projecting from the wall, with no doorway or window.
only beneath it is impure. For the projection with a handbreadth interposes against the impurity.
extends beyond the lower one by a handbreadth. The upper projection is longer than the lower by a handbreadth.
beneath them. Beneath the lower projection and beneath the excess.
and impurity beneath it. Beneath the lower projection.

beneath it and between them is impure. Although the excess itself does not have a handbreadth opening, it joins the rest of the upper projection to complete it to a handbreadth, and therefore the impurity spreads through it between the projections (Rosh, Oholot 14:5).

but beneath the lower one is pure. Since there is no handbreadth beneath the excess, the impurity does not spread from it beneath the lower projection (and the excess does not combine with the lower projection, since it does not continue it).
and between them there is no handbreadth. There is no tent-height of space beneath the upper projection, and therefore it does not interpose against the impurity beneath it.
only beneath it is impure. Since the lower projection is a handbreadth or more above the ground, it is a tent and interposes against the impurity.
opposite the impurity up to the sky is impure. And it does not break through downward to the depths, since the tent beneath it interposes.
for it is crushed. For any impurity that is not beneath a handbreadth is crushed (above 16:6).

and likewise two curtains etc.. Their law is like the law of the projections. Although they receive impurity, they interpose when they are made into tents (Mishnah Acharonah, Oholot 14:7, and see above 13:3; and see a different explanation in Tiferet Yisrael, ibid., Boaz, note 6).

if the impurity was a handbreadth above the ground, the vessel on top of it... brings the impurity. Since there is a handbreadth of height here, the vessel above the impurity is considered a tent and defiles all the vessels beneath it (similar to above, end of chapter 16). But when the impurity is not a handbreadth above the ground, it is considered crushed impurity that breaks upward (see Merkevet HaMishneh). Some explain that in every case where the upper vessel spreading over the impurity is a handbreadth high, it brings the impurity to the vessels beneath it, even when the impurity itself is not a handbreadth high (Kesef Mishneh; and see Ra'avad).
touching each other by their corners. The corner of one board touches the corner of the other.

like one who touches vessels that touched a corpse's tent. He is impure with evening-impurity (Merkevet HaMishneh, based on Tosefta Oholot 15:1; compare Rambam's wording below 18:7). According to most commentators the meaning here is that he is impure with seven-day impurity, which is the law in the Mishnah (Oholot 15:2).
but all the vessels that we said bring the impurity etc.. See above 13:4.
as we explained. Above 12:1.

and their impurity is as vessels that spread over a corpse. They are impure with seven-day impurity, and not as vessels that touch a corpse's tent, whose degree of impurity is lower (for the degrees of impurity see above chapter 5).
a jar. Made of clay.
sitting on its base in the open air. Resting in its normal position with no tent over it.
beneath it opposite its airspace. Beneath its cavity and not beneath its wall.
beneath the thickness of its wall. For example, the jar's wall is thick and the impurity is buried beneath it.
and a clay vessel becomes impure only from its airspace. As above 6:3.
impurity breaks upward and breaks downward. And one who spreads opposite the impurity becomes impure.

if there was a handbreadth in the walls. The walls of the vessel are a handbreadth thick, and the impurity is partly beneath the wall and partly beneath the jar's cavity (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 9:16; and see Ma'ayanei Yehoshua, Oholot 9:16, and Sidrei Taharot, Oholot 147:1, who described the structure of the jar differently).

all of it is impure, and opposite its mouth is pure. Everything that touches the walls is impure, whereas what is in the vessel's cavity is pure (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.; even what spreads over part of the olive's bulk is pure; see Sidrei Taharot, ibid.). The reason the impurity spreads through all the walls is unclear (see Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid., and it requires further study).
in what case does this apply? To a pure jar. One sitting on its base in the air, in which the impurity breaks upward and breaks downward and one who touches all of it is not impure.
but if it was impure. For an impure vessel does not interpose against impurity (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 9:16).
or a handbreadth above the ground or covered or inverted on its mouth etc.. In these cases the jar becomes a vessel that spreads over the impurity (see also below 19:5).

everything is impure and whoever touches any of it is impure. Although a clay vessel, even when impure through a corpse, does not make people and vessels impure (above 5:6), here one who touches it becomes impure (for the reason see Piskei VeShitot).
if it was encircled with a tight seal. It has a tight, secure cover that saves what is inside it from becoming impure by tent (see below 21:1).
and the vessels on top of it are impure. Although the jar saves the foods and liquids by the law of a tight seal, it does not interpose against crushed impurity.
or lying on their sides. Lying lengthwise.
in the air. With no tent over them.
and they touch each other with a handbreadth opening. Where the jars touch each other there is a space of a handbreadth by a handbreadth.

but if they were impure. Since they are impure, even though there is no handbreadth of height beneath them they bring the impurity, because their upper side becomes like a tent (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 15:3; and see also above 16:7). But if they were pure this could not be said, since a clay vessel does not become impure from its back (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.).
or touched a corpse. With one hand.
and spread over the vessels. With his other hand.
if his hand has a handbreadth. Then it is considered a tent and brings the impurity.
and in them are two halves of olives' bulk. Each one has the measure of half an olive's bulk of a corpse, which does not defile by tent.
and everything became one tent and he and the houses became impure. The tent combines the halves that defile by tent when divided (above 4:8), and now there is the measure that defiles.
brings the impurity to the house. This person is considered a tent partly over the impurity and partly inside the house (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 11:4).
lying on the threshold. Lying on the threshold of the house.
because a person is hollow etc.. As above 16:7.

and since the impurity spread over him, it is as if he spreads over it etc.. The impure person does not interpose, so the impurity above him passes through him, and thus his upper side spreads over the impurity (see above, ibid.) and brings it into the house.

because he is like one spreading over the impurity, and a person brings and does not interpose. The person lying down is considered a tent over the impurity, and therefore everything on top of him is impure.
as we explained. Above 12:1, 13:4.
who passed through it under the akhsadra. And the akhsadra reaches the doorway of the house.
and one of them closed the door and propped it with the key. He held the door shut with the key in his hand (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 6:2).
if the door can stand on its own etc.. See also above 15:2.
and the person and the vessels bring and do not interpose, as we explained. Above 12:1, 13:4.

and its eye is vaulted outward. The eye of an oven is an opening at the bottom of the oven through which fire is put in and ashes taken out (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 5:1). Here the eye is made like a tube extending outside the house.
the oven is impure. The eye is considered part of the oven, and since the impurity spread over part of the oven, all of it became impure (Commentary on the Mishnah, ibid.; and see Piskei VeShitot).
for the oven is not high enough above the ground to bring impurity into the house. Since the oven's eye is not a handbreadth above the ground, the impurity does not enter the house.
a migdal that comes in measure. A large, stationary wooden cabinet (for its definition see above 6:2), which interposes against impurity (above 13:3).

that stands in the doorway and opens outward. It stands entirely in the space of the doorway and its doors face the exit (for example, the migdal fills the entire space of the doorway so that the impurity has no way out except through it; Kesef Mishneh).
and the way of impurity is to go out. Therefore what is inside the migdal is impure, since it stands at the exit from the house.
makhni. A drawer.

pulled toward its rear and projecting less than a handbreadth. The drawer extends from the rear side of the cabinet toward the house and is open slightly, so that there is no handbreadth opening there.
and cannot be removed. It cannot be taken out of the migdal.
and impurity is in it opposite the beams. In the drawer beneath the opening, so that it is opposite the beams of the house's ceiling.
and the house is impure. For crushed impurity within a tent spreads throughout the entire tent (see above 7:7).
or in its chest. In its lower compartment.
even though there is no handbreadth in its exit, the house is impure. Since the migdal stands within the house, the impurity goes out even where there is no handbreadth opening (see also below 19:3).
if there is a handbreadth there, they are impure. For the impurity in the house spreads there.
for I regard the beams as if they came down and blocked it. Since the gap between the migdal and the ceiling is small, the impurity does not spread there.
it was standing in the open air. The cabinet is outside the house, so there is no tent over it.
vessels that are in its thickness. Vessels that are within the thickness of its walls.
a tent that slopes downward and tapers to the height of a finger. The tent becomes lower until it is a finger's height from the ground (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 7:2).
vessels beneath the slope are impure. Even though there is no handbreadth there, since the slope is considered part of the tent.
the impurity from within the slope. Beneath it.
one who touches it from within. One who touches the slope from its inner side.

is impure with seven-day impurity. For a corpse's tent is impure with seven-day impurity, like a vessel that touched a corpse (above 5:12), and one who touches a vessel that a corpse touched is also impure with seven-day impurity (ibid., halakhah 3).
as if it were a vessel that touched the tent. One who touches this vessel is impure only with evening-impurity (see ibid., halakhah 4).
on the back of the slope. Placed on it from the outside.
one who touches it from behind is impure with seven-day impurity. Like one who touches vessels that touched a corpse.
and one who touches the slope from within is impure with evening-impurity. Like one who touches vessels that touched vessels that touched a corpse.
about half an olive's bulk from within and half an olive's bulk from behind etc.. In this case both sides of the slope become like vessels that touched the tent.

and the tent itself is impure with seven-day impurity. Unlike one who touches the sheet, who is sometimes impure with evening-impurity, the tent's sheet itself is impure for seven days in every case. (From the Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 7:2, it appears that this law refers to one who touches the tent itself, who is always impure with seven-day impurity; see Piskei VeShitot.)
the tent's flap spread out on the ground. The edge of the tent lies on the ground.
impurity breaks upward and breaks downward. Like the law of crushed impurity.
a beehive. Made of wood, which is a large, hollow vessel.
and it is in the doorway of the house with its mouth outward. It lies within the space of the doorway and its opening faces outside the house.
and an olive's bulk of a corpse is placed beneath it or on top of it outside. On the part of the hive that is outside the house.
anything opposite the olive's bulk, beneath it or on top of it, is impure. Like the law of crushed impurity.
and everything in the airspace inside it is pure, except a vessel opposite the impurity. For the hive is a vessel and does not interpose.
but vessels inside it or beneath it or on top of it. In the part of the hive that is outside the house.
are pure. Since the mouth of the hive faces outward, it does not extend the house's tent, and therefore does not bring the impurity to vessels outside it.
everything in the house and everything in it. Since the impurity is inside the hive, it spreads through the hive's cavity and enters the house.

and everything on top of it and everything beneath it opposite the impurity. For the vessel does not interpose against the impurity. And although when the impurity is beneath a vessel that spreads over it, it brings the impurity to everything beneath and above it (as above 12:1), here, where the impurity is inside the vessel, it brings the impurity only to the vessel's cavity and not to what is above and below it (see the article by M. Y. Ben Gershom, Ma'aliyot 25, p. 172).
as we explained. Above 12:1 (that a vessel does not interpose against impurity).

or on top of it, everything is impure etc.. The hive becomes a tent that brings the impurity to what is beneath it, into the house. Even when the impurity is on top of the hive, since the hive does not interpose, the impurity descends into the space beneath it, and from there spreads into the house.

but everything in the airspace inside it is pure. Even though there is a handbreadth tent beneath the hive, the impurity does not enter from there into the air inside it. It may be explained that when a vessel spreads over impurity beneath it, since it becomes a tent in its entirety, its inner cavity is not taken into account, and therefore the impurity does not spread there (see the article mentioned above, p. 176). As for what is above it, the law is not stated here; however, in some editions it says that everything on top of it is also impure (and so it appears from the Mishnah, Oholot 9:2).
and everything beneath it and everything on top of it. Even if not opposite the impurity.
for vessels or a person that became a tent over the impurity. For example, here, where the hive is a handbreadth above the ground.
bring and do not interpose. Therefore not only what is inside it is impure, but also everything beneath it and everything on top of it.
as we explained. Above 12:1.
and mechulchelet. Hollow (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 9:3).
for it is not a vessel. An incomplete hive is not considered a vessel even if the gap was plugged with straw (Hilchot Kelim 14:11).
afutzah. Full.
so that there is not found in it a space of a handbreadth in one place. In such a case it is not considered a vessel.
because it is a wooden tent and not a vessel. Therefore it interposes against the impurity.
only its inside is impure. As with a tent that brings the impurity and interposes.
if it was on top of it, opposite it up to the sky is impure. And the impurity does not break downward, since the hive is not a vessel and it interposes.
if it was resting on the ground. This hive that is not a vessel.

and an olive's bulk of a corpse is placed beneath it, opposite it down to the depths is impure. Although the impurity is crushed beneath the hive, it does not break upward to the sky. It seems this should be explained thus: since this hive is not a vessel but a tent, even though it does not spread over the impurity, it interposes against it (see the article mentioned above, pp. 178-179).
anything opposite the olive's bulk beneath it or on top of it is impure etc.. As above, halakhah 1.

if the impurity was inside it or in the house, everything is impure. Everything in it and everything in the house, and everything on top of it and beneath it, even not opposite the impurity. And although in the parallel case above, halakhah 1, when the impurity was inside the hive only what was opposite the impurity above and below was impure, in this case everything is impure. It seems that since its mouth is open to the house, it is considered one tent with the house, so that the tent-impurity in the house passes through the hive and spreads to what is above and below it.
as was explained. Above, halakhah 1.

except what is on top of it. Since the hive is not a vessel and interposes against the impurity, the impurity does not pass to its top. But what is beneath it is impure, since there is a handbreadth tent there and the impurity enters it from the house.
and its mouth is upward toward the beams of the house. Its opening faces the ceiling.
impurity in the house, what is inside it is pure. For example, the hive is not a vessel, so it interposes against the impurity (Chasdei David, Kuntres Torat HaOhel, 19).
for the way of impurity is to go out within the house in less than a handbreadth. As above 18:4.
for the way of impurity is to go out. Therefore when the impurity is in the house, what is inside the hive is impure, even when there is no handbreadth opening between them.
and its way is not to enter. Therefore when the impurity is inside the hive, even though its opening does not face outward, it does not enter the house.
lying on its side in the air. Lying on its side outside the house, with no tent over it.
anything opposite the olive's bulk, beneath it and on top of it, is impure etc.. As above, halakhah 1.
and everything opposite the impurity etc.. Only what is opposite the impurity is impure and no more, since the hive is attached to the ground, as above ibid.

but what is inside it is pure, except a vessel opposite the impurity. Even though there is a handbreadth tent beneath the hive, the impurity does not enter from there into the air inside it (for the reason see the explanation of the parallel case in halakhah 1).
and everything beneath it and everything above it on top of it. Even if not opposite the impurity.
as we explained. Above 12:1.
incomplete and plugged with straw. Then it is not a vessel.
or it comes in measure. Large and stationary (see above 6:2); then it interposes against the impurity.
opposite it down to the depths is impure. And the impurity does not break upward, since the hive interposes.
for we already explained etc.. Above 13:3.
and it is sitting on its base. Resting in its normal position on its bottom.
impurity breaks upward and breaks downward. Like the law of any impurity that has no tent over it.
but if it was a handbreadth high or covered or inverted on its mouth etc.. Now the hive is a vessel that spreads, which brings the impurity to everything above and below it (see also above 17:6).

if the impurity was below. From Rambam's words in the Commentary on the Mishnah (Oholot 9:13) it appears that this condition refers only to cases of covered or inverted on its mouth (in which cases the hive is considered a sealed grave that defiles from every side). However, from Rambam's words here it seems that even where the hive is covered or inverted on its mouth it is treated as a vessel that spreads over the impurity, so that it does not matter where the impurity is, and in any case everything is impure (and indeed the Chazon Ish, Oholot 2:23, wrote that the words 'if the impurity was below' appear superfluous).
as we explained. Above 12:1.
a camel standing in the air. With no tent over it.
vessels on its back are pure. For the tent of a domestic or wild animal interposes against impurity (above 12:1, 13:3).
if it was crouching. Sitting, and now there is no space of a handbreadth beneath it.
it breaks upward and breaks downward. Like the law of crushed impurity.
we already explained in Nezirut. Hilchot Nezirut 7:6.
even though he became impure with seven-day impurity. Because they spread over him and over the corpse.
he does not shave. He does not nullify the days of his naziriteship and does not shave his hair and bring offerings (see ibid. 6:3).
and from there you learn that all these laws of tent-impurity... are rabbinic. For any corpse impurity for which a nazirite does not shave is not Torah law (above 3:3).
words of tradition. A tradition of the Sages.

and one is not liable to karet for them for entering the Temple or eating its sacrificial foods. A person who became impure through them and entered the Temple or deliberately ate sacrificial foods is not liable to karet like other impure people (see Hilchot Bi'at HaMikdash 3:12; Hilchot Pesulei HaMukdashin 18:13).

but only with regard to the impurity of terumah and sacrificial foods. He is considered impure for seven days in that he is forbidden to eat terumah and sacrificial foods, and if he touches them they become impure.
as we explained. Above 5:5.
tight seal. A cover of a vessel that is tight and secure on it (explained below 21:1).
and absorbed. In the body of a living creature, as explained later in the chapter.
everything inside the vessel is pure. If it is a clay vessel or a vessel that cannot become impure (ibid.).
even a person. Who, unlike a dog, receives impurity.
the ring is pure. From tent-impurity, because it is absorbed (and likewise pure from the impurity of touching a person, since that is a touch of the hidden places, see below 25:12).
and if they died with the flesh of a corpse in their intestines. And they are in a pure house.
or the vessels. Are in their intestines, and they are in an impure house.

most of one was slaughtered in a bird and most of two in an animal. The measure of valid slaughter in a bird is most of one organ (the windpipe or gullet), and in an animal most of both organs (Hilchot Shechitah 1:9).
twitching. Moving their limbs.
and how long may the impurity remain in their intestines. How much time may pass from when they ate the impurity for it still to defile if they die.
in a dog, three days, from time to time. A dog digests the impurity in its intestines only after this period.
and he vomited it through the excretory passage. He expelled it as excrement after digestion.
the flesh is pure and the bones remain in their impurity. The bones are hard and do not digest, unlike flesh, which is soft.
visible into the jar and not projecting into its airspace. They are embedded in the stopper on its inner side so that they can be seen from inside, but they do not protrude into the jar's cavity.
pure. Like the vessels absorbed in the plaster of an oven.
as will be explained. Below 23:1.
and if there is beneath them something like a garlic peel. Any thickness of stopper.
even though they sink into its airspace. That is, they protrude inward into the jar but there is a layer of stopper over them.
these are pure. For they are not considered inside the jar.
as we explained. Above, halakhot 2-4.
a spindle in which the metal tzenira was absorbed. A wooden spinning implement whose hook at its head sank into it (see Hilchot Parah 12:10).
and a malmad. A stick used to direct oxen.
the darban. The nail at the head of the goad.
for things absorbed in vessels are saved only by a tight seal. Things absorbed in vessels are saved only when those vessels are encircled by a tight seal (as explained below).
in the plaster of the oven. Clay put on it for repairing or reinforcing it (see Hilchot Kelim 15:7).
or impurity fell into its airspace. For an oven is a clay vessel that receives impurity from its airspace.

since the oven is pure, so too the vessels etc.. Although there is no law of absorption for vessels, here the law differs: since the tight seal saves the oven itself, it also saves the vessels absorbed in it.
in the stopper of the jar. In the jar's cover made of clay.
from its side. Opposite the jar's walls.

these are impure. The jar's walls do not need clay, so the needle or ring absorbed there is not considered absorbed in a vessel encircled with a tight seal but as placed outside it (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 9:1).
from opposite its mouth. Opposite the jar's cavity.
unlike its walls, as will be explained. The walls of the tent are not considered like it, as explained below 24:4-8.
for they are under another tent. A handbreadth by a handbreadth by a handbreadth is called a tent and interposes against impurity (above 12:1).
from the side of its ground. Facing the ground and close to it (and see below 24:2 regarding a partition built upward inside a house).
as we explained. Above, halakhah 1.
they are as if buried in the floor of the house and impure. For at less than a handbreadth in height it is not considered a tent.
a drain that is vaulted beneath the house and has a handbreadth opening. A covered sewer channel passing beneath the house, with a cavity a handbreadth in diameter.

impurity in it, the house is pure; impurity in the house, what is in it is pure. For example, the opening of the drain into the house is closed by a cover or bars so that the impurity does not pass from it into the house or vice versa (Responsa Chatam Sofer, part 2, Yoreh De'ah 340; Sidrei Taharot, Oholot 81:2).
at its outlet. At the opening outside the house.

and the impurity was in it, the house is impure. Since the drain's outlet does not have the measure of a handbreadth opening, the impurity has no way out of the drain except through the opening inside the house (even though it is covered), and therefore the house is impure (Chatam Sofer, ibid.).
for the way of impurity is not to enter. Therefore, although impurity in the drain goes out into the house, impurity in the house does not enter the drain.
it does not have a handbreadth... impurity in the house, what is in it is impure etc.. Since the drain's height does not have the measure of a handbreadth, it is treated like the floor of the house.
and like half an olive's bulk. The measure of half an olive's bulk of a corpse.
for there is an olive's bulk in the house. For the tent combines the divided impurities (above 4:8).
and a tight seal does not protect against impurity. A tight seal does not prevent impurity from defiling (above, halakhah 1).
for they are open to one another and to the house. The exit from the inner room leads to the middle room, and the exit from the middle room leads to the outer room (the house).
the outer is impure and the inner and middle are pure. Since only in the outer room does the impurity combine to the measure of an olive's bulk.
for the way of impurity is to go out and not to enter. See also above 18:4, 19:3.
tight seal. A cover of a vessel that is tight and secure on it.
and from the oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages.

for Scripture speaks only of a clay vessel... which becomes impure only through its opening. As explained above 6:3 (and see Hilchot Kelim 13:1), unlike other vessels that receive impurity from their back.
therefore if its opening was sealed... it saved everything inside it. Since the vessel itself is pure, it saves everything inside it from becoming impure.
all the more so for all vessels that do not receive impurity. If a clay vessel, which receives impurity, saves with a tight seal, then vessels that do not receive impurity certainly save.
dung vessels... and a wooden vessel that comes in measure. See above 6:1-2; Hilchot Kelim 1:2-3, 1:6.
and wooden planks that are flat and not vessels. They have no receptacle and are not used as vessels (see Hilchot Kelim 1:10, 4:1).
and unfinished metal vessels. Metal vessels whose manufacture was not completed (see ibid. 8:1-2).
all the more so absorbed things. Which are buried more deeply.
and vessels beneath tents. Which are in a separate domain.
and tents save by covering alone. Even by a cover that is not securely attached.
a funnel that he inverted. He turned it on its mouth so that its narrow opening is upward.
saves by covering. Since he inverted it on its mouth, it is like a tent that saves by covering alone and does not need a tight seal (and see below, halakhah 3).
even though a part of it has a small hole. Its end (the spout) is open and has no cover.
it is like sealed. The spout is not considered an opening, since it is very small and is made not for putting in but for taking out.
if he did not smear a tight seal on the sides. He did not stick the vessel to the ground with one of the materials considered a tight seal (explained below 22:8).
because they are like a tent. Since they have the measure of a handbreadth opening, their law is that of a tent that saves even without a tight seal, and even down to the depths.
a jar. Made of clay.
everything beneath it is impure. For it does not save in a corpse's tent.
if he stuck its mouth to the wall and smeared the sides, it saves everything inside it. In this case the tight seal is regarded as being 'upon it' (Kiryat Sefer).
and everything opposite it in the wall. If there is a cavity in the wall opposite the jar, everything in that cavity is also saved by the jar (Rabbi Shimshon, Kelim 10:1).
for a clay vessel does not save as a tent. Only when it is encircled with a tight seal.
as we explained. In the previous paragraph.
a beam that has a handbreadth. Which brings the impurity beneath all of it.

the vessels in the pot are pure, for they were saved by the tent's cover over them. Although a clay vessel does not save as a tent (above, halakhah 3), in this case the vessels in the pot are pure because it is attached to the beam, so the vessels in it are considered as not under the corpse's tent (Chiddushei HaGrach on the Mishnah, Oholot 6:2; and see Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 5:7).
on a smooth board. That has no sides at all, and is therefore not considered a vessel and saves in every case (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 5:6).
chadut. A pool, like a pit but with walls rising above the ground (Commentary on the Mishnah, Rosh Hashanah 3:5 and elsewhere).
and its flower projects and covers the mouth of the chadut. The upper part of the lamp, shaped like a wide plate, covers the opening of the chadut.

and vessels between the rim of the vessel and the rim of the chadut. For example, the chadut's wall is thick, and the vessels are placed on the thickness of the wall between the inner rim of the chadut and the rim of the saving vessel.
are pure down to the depths. All the vessels opposite the saving vessel are pure even when they are deep in the ground.
and if not, all are impure. For a tent that rests on vessels neither saves nor interposes against impurity (above 12:1).
as we explained. Above 20:1.
vessels in the walls of the chadut. It seems that in this case the chadut is adjacent to one of the walls of the house, and the vessels are placed in the chadut's wall shared with the house's wall.
if in their place there is a handbreadth by a handbreadth by a handbreadth, they are pure. Since in their place there is the measure of a tent that saves them from the impurity.
and if not, they are impure. Since they are judged as vessels in the wall of the house (which, when in its inner half, are impure, as below 24:4-5; and see Tosefta Oholot 12:6).
and if the walls of the chadut were wider than those of a house. The chadut has a wall of its own even on the side adjacent to the house's wall.
we already explained. Above 12:3.
for an old oven. One that has been fired once and now receives impurity (see Hilchot Kelim 15:1).
and they do not become tents. Like other clay vessels (above, halakhah 3).
and likewise we explained etc.. Above 12:3.
an old oven inside a new one. And they are in a corpse's tent.
and if not, everything is pure. Since the cover rests firmly on the new oven, this oven is considered a covered tent that saves everything inside it.
and it extends beyond the mouth of the oven. It rests on the oven and projects on all its sides.
and is encircled with a tight seal. The sarida and the oven are joined to each other with a tight seal.
impurity beneath it or on top of it. Placed beneath the projecting part of the sarida or on top of it.
for everything is impure. Since the sarida rests on an old oven, it brings the impurity to everything beneath and above it and does not interpose against the impurity (see above 12:3).
then what is opposite the oven's airspace is pure. Since the tight seal saves what is in the oven, it saves what is opposite it.

the impurity was opposite the oven's airspace. Lying on the sarida opposite the oven's cavity (and see Arukh HaShulchan HaAtid 46:24, where the sarida is inverted on its mouth and therefore saves, as below, halakhah 11).

a pot that he inverted on the mouth of the jar. He turned the pot so its mouth faces downward and covered the opening of the jar with it. The case is where the jar and pot are clay vessels placed in a corpse's tent.
saves everything in it. That is placed in the jar.
and what is between it and the rims of the jar. Between the inner wall of the pot and the outer rim of the jar.
he set it on the mouth of the jar in the usual way and smeared. He stuck the pot's bottom to the jar's mouth with a tight seal.
as we explained. Above, halakhah 1.
bases of large vessels. The bottoms of large clay vessels with a small receptacle used for gripping (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 2:2).
and the bases of pointed-bottom vessels. The ends of vessels whose bottoms are pointed (ibid.).
and their walls behind them. The walls of vessels that have a hollow on their rear side.
he scraped and smoothed them. He smoothed and polished them.
and if he sank the vessels in it, it saves. When it is encircled with a tight seal (Kesef Mishneh).

until it is pierced with a hole the size of a pomegranate's exit, and in a large one until most of it is breached. From this measure on, the vessel no longer saves even when the hole is plugged (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 9:8).
with the size of a pomegranate's exit. A hole large enough for a pomegranate to pass through (for this measure see Hilchot Kelim 6:2).
even though it is not considered a vessel for impurity. For the measure of a hole in a clay vessel with regard to impurity is at most that of olives' exit (see ibid. 19:2).
and how much must the hole be etc.. See also Hilchot Kelim 14:9, 19:1.
its measure is the size of an olive's exit. A hole through which an olive can pass.
its measure is that of absorbing liquid. That if the vessel is placed in liquid, the liquid will penetrate the vessel through this hole.
sarida. The cover of an oven.

the full mouth of a goad. The size equal to the thickness of the ox goad used to drive the animal (and perhaps it also served for stirring the fire in the oven, and therefore they measured by it; Tiferet Yisrael, Kelim 9:7).

if the crack was round etc.. If the crack is shaped so that the goad cannot enter it, even though the circumference measure of the crack equals that of the goad, the oven is not impure as long as the goad cannot actually enter it (the commentators had difficulty understanding the situation discussed here, since the goad's shape is round, and explained it in different ways).
in the eye of an oven that is plastered. In its side opening through which wood is kindled, which is stopped with clay.
the fullness of a spindle that enters and leaves while burning. That one can put in and take out of the hole a stick with a gap such that if it is burning it will not be extinguished by this.
the second joint of a rye stalk. The second segment of the rye stalk, which is thinner than the first segment near the ground (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 9:8).
and chatzavim. Jugs.
a reed. The common reed plant.
when they were made for wine. Barrels and jugs of wine are customarily pierced to let the air out, and therefore the hole must be large enough for this purpose.
but if they were made by people, even any amount renders them impure. Since the hole was made deliberately by a person, even a smaller measure counts.
and a menikit. A bent small tube passing through a hole in the wall of the jar, made for sucking from it (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 9:2; and see Hilchot Ma'achalot Asurot 12:11).
the jar and the liquids are pure. Although the jar has a hole, the menikit plugs it.

and even though it is bent, the bent one is not like sealed. Although the menikit is bent so that the end inside the jar is not open to the corpse's tent, it is not considered a sealed vessel because of this, since its other end is open to the corpse's tent in any case.
he sealed half the hole and plugged half. He smeared clay over half the hole and plugged the other half with lees and the like.
with a twig. A splinter.
with wooden nails. Which do not receive impurity.
or he wrapped around them cork pieces. He wrapped them in cork bark (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 10:6).
and with gypsum. Plaster.
with lead. Tin (a kind of metal).
a cord but not tight. A cover that is not tight.
with a fat dried fig that has not been rendered susceptible. A fig that has not been rendered susceptible to impurity by a liquid (see Hilchot Tumat Ochlin 1:1-2).
with fruit juices. Which do not render susceptible to impurity (ibid. 1:3).
for an impure thing does not interpose. See also above 13:4.
that became loosened. Became slightly loosened from its place.
that he placed on the mouth of the jar. He plugged the mouth of the jar with a ball or bundle made of a material called gome.

it does not save until he smears over the entire ball and the entire bundle from bottom to top. Since the ball and bundle are not completely airtight, the jar does not save as long as they have not been smeared over their whole surface with one of the surrounding materials.
if it was of paper or leather. Which are airtight materials.
with a string. A thread.
if he smeared from the sides, it saves. And he need not smear over them.
a skin bag of fish hide. Which does not receive impurity and saves in a corpse's tent (above 21:2).
with which he clothed the jar and tied it from below. He wrapped the jar in a skin bag or paper and tied it from below.
a pitched jar. Coated inside with pitch.
that the clay peeled off from above. The clay peeled off the upper part of the jar, leaving only the pitch layer.
and pressed it until it stuck to the pitch. He pressed the cover to the pitch until it stuck.
the base of the jar. The lower part of the jar that did not peel.
and likewise with muries vessels and the like, of things that can be smeared. Vessels in which one puts fish brine or other oily foods that stick to the vessel's walls.
for the smeared substance was between the cover and the vessel like a wreath. The fat overflowed on the walls and surrounded their top, and thereby sticks the cover to them.
all vessels that save with a tight seal. Clay vessels, and likewise vessels that do not receive impurity (see above 21:1).
and washable vessels. Vessels that are purified in a mikveh (except clay vessels).
like other vessels that save. Just as other vessels that do not receive impurity and save with a tight seal also save the washable vessels and garments inside them.
and a clay vessel receives impurity. When it is open.
and an impure vessel does not interpose. And if it was encircled with a tight seal it does not save.
and all vessels of amei ha'aretz are presumed impure. Because they are not expert and careful in the laws of impurity and purity.
as will be explained. Hilchot Matmei Mishkav UMoshav 10:1.
of an am ha'aretz does not save everything. Since his vessels are presumed impure.
a chaver. A person who is careful about impurities and purities.
they are impure by the am ha'aretz's account. They are considered impure since they are in his possession.
and waits for sunset. He waits until evening arrives after their immersion and they become pure.
and use it for pure things and come to a mishap. For it requires sprinkling of the purification water on the third and seventh days and does not become pure by immersion and nightfall.

and because of this they decreed etc.. And now there is no concern for a mishap, for an am ha'aretz does not imagine that a washable vessel is saved by a clay vessel's tight seal; therefore if he says the vessel is pure from corpse impurity he is believed (see Hilchot Matmei Mishkav UMoshav 11:12, that an am ha'aretz is believed regarding corpse impurity).
even if he made it a golel for a grave. Although one who touches it is impure with seven-day impurity, it itself and what is in it are pure (above 6:4).
. The order of halakhot 2-3 in the printed editions is the reverse of their order in the manuscripts.
for they are used with the ashes of the red heifer. To sanctify the purification water and sprinkle it.
or with sacrificial foods. For example, to put libations in them and the like.
amei ha'aretz are believed about their purity. See also Hilchot Parah 13:12; Hilchot Matmei Mishkav UMoshav 11:1.
an aruvah. An opening in the ceiling.
and a pot. Made of clay.
and pierced to the size that absorbs liquid. A pot is a vessel also made for liquid, and therefore with a hole of this size it does not save by the law of a tight seal (above 22:3).

and the upper room is pure. Although the pierced pot does not save by the law of a tight seal, it now saves by the law of interposing in a corpse's tent (see Tosafot Yom Tov, Kelim 9:8; and although the pot became impure and an impure vessel does not interpose, since it was not impure before, with respect to the upper room it is still considered pure and interposes, like a clay vessel that does not become impure from its back).

if it was whole... as if it were under a tight seal in a clay vessel. Since the pot is whole, it saves by the law of a tight seal (and not by the law of interposing in a tent), and therefore it saves only things that a clay vessel saves with a tight seal.
because it is common. For it is the way of a person to be in an upper room.
in a trough. A large bowl.
it separated and returned and touched it, it made it impure. Now the dough became impure by touching one impure through a corpse.
as we explained. Above 21:1.
and therefore the touch of an am ha'aretz does not make them impure. And there is no concern for the mishap mentioned above, halakhah 1.
and part of it is spread over the aruvah. The edges of the tent are spread over the opening of the aruvah.
even though its roof is not over the aruvah. The tent's roof is not aligned with the opening of the aruvah, so that there is no handbreadth opening between the opening and the tent's sheet.
a house that he divided with pure jars. He built inside it a partition of pure clay jars.
from the ground to the beams. From the floor to the ceiling.
if the mouth of the jars faces the pure side, these save. For a clay vessel does not become impure from its back (as above 15:4, 16:5).
he plastered with clay, either inside or outside. He plastered clay on them (where the mouths of the jars face the impurity) opposite their mouths or opposite their bases.
if the clay can stand on its own, it saves. See also above 15:2.
and if not, it does not save. When the clay cannot stand on its own, the jars are the main partition, and they do not interpose against impurity when their openings face it.
and everything is one tent. The whole house is considered one tent as if it had no partition.
or with sheets. That interpose against impurity (see above 13:3).
if he divided it from the sides or from the direction of the beams. If the partition is built next to the wall or the ceiling.
vessels between the partition... are pure. The partition saves the pure ones from becoming impure.
as we explained regarding a tent inside a house. Above 20:1.
within the thickness of the partition itself. For example, there is a small hole in the partition and the vessels are placed in it (Chazon Ish, Oholot 13:4).

if the place of the vessels was a handbreadth by a handbreadth, they are impure etc.. Like the law of a window between one house and another, where the impurity passes through it only if it has a handbreadth opening (above 14:1).
and we already explained. Above 20:6.

all the vessels opposite the exit of the impurity in the full width of the doorway are impure. The impurity in the straw goes out of the house through the doorway, so all the vessels there become impure.

if in their place there is a handbreadth by a handbreadth by a handbreadth, they are pure, and if not, impure. Since there is no handbreadth opening between the straw and the beams, the house's tent does not spread over the vessels inside the straw; therefore they are pure when their place has a space of a handbreadth by a handbreadth that makes them count as a place of their own. But when their place has no space of a handbreadth, they are impure even though there is no tent over them, like vessels in a wall on which the house's roof rests (see below, halakhah 5, for explanation).

and if there is a handbreadth opening between the straw and the beams, either way they are impure. Since there is a handbreadth opening between the straw and the ceiling, the house's tent spreads over the vessels in the straw, and the straw does not interpose.
a house near the impurity is impure. And everything in it becomes impure with tent-impurity.
maaziva. The layer of clay and stones on top of a wooden ceiling (and see below, halakhah 8).
if the maaziva was open to the air. There is no upper room over the house.
even opposite the impurity it is pure, for the impurity spread throughout the house. The impurity is considered as being inside the house, so that it interposes against it.

for it is impossible to be exact. Since one cannot determine the exact midpoint, it must be assumed that the impurity is closer to one of the sides, and therefore neither side can be declared pure with certainty.
a wall that is open to the air. That has no roof on it.
and it is not mounted on the wall. For where the roof is mounted on the wall, the entire wall is judged as part of the house (as above 7:7).

half and half, the house is impure and the one standing above is pure, for the impurity spread in the house. Although in the earlier cases of half and half everything is impure, here it cannot be said, since impurity spreading sideways toward the house cannot also break upward at the same time (see Chasdei David, Oholot 7:8; Mayim Tehorim, Oholot 6:4, Charedim note 2).
even from its half inward the house is pure. Since the wall is exposed to the air.
a house that uses the wall. An underground house or one hewn in rock, whose excavation created the wall.
like a garlic peel. Any thickness.

from this you have learned that a built wall is judged half and half, and a rock wall... is judged as a garlic peel. The reason seems to be that such a wall, created by excavation from its sides, is not considered a wall but ordinary ground, which interposes against impurity (see Tiferet Yisrael, Oholot 6:6).
for half its thickness is building and half is rock. For example, the rock was thin and he built a structure next to it.
is judged half and half. Like a wall serving the house.
between the beams of the house. Between the wooden ceiling beams lying beneath the maaziva layer.

and we regard the impurity as if it were crushed in the ground and it defiles opposite it only. Since the layer of beams is normally sealed like the ground, the impurity within it is considered crushed. This is unlike the maaziva layer, which although above the beams, since it is not as sealed, is considered part of the building and is judged half and half (above, halakhah 4; Kesef Mishneh; and see Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 6:5).

and if in its place there is a handbreadth by a handbreadth, everything is impure. For where there is a space of a handbreadth in the place of the impurity, it is considered a sealed grave that defiles from all around (above 7:4), and therefore everything is impure (the house, and also the upper room above it if there is one).

and likewise if it was visible inside the house. If the ceiling beneath the impurity is transparent (Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 6:5), or if there is not even a garlic peel's thickness beneath it (Rabbi Shimshon and Rosh, ibid.; Kesef Mishneh).
two doorways one above the other. For example, a house doorway and an upper room doorway.
if it appears to be within one of them. It is in a place that appears to belong more to one of the doorways, even though in fact it is closer to the other.
and if not, they are judged half and half. We follow the location of the impurity: if it is in the half closer to one of them, that one is impure and the other pure.
a pillar standing in the house and crushed impurity beneath it. The impurity is buried under the floor opposite the pillar.
and it defiles only opposite the impurity. And the rest of the house is pure, since the impurity is not inside it.
peraḥ. A building ornament shaped like a flower projecting at the top of the pillar.
it is. The entire pillar.
like a sealed grave and defiles from all around. For the entire height of the structure built over a handbreadth of space is considered a grave (above 7:4).
and the entire house is impure, for it spread over the grave. Even though it does not spread over the impurity itself.
all the upper rooms built on this wall etc.. The wall is tall and serves all the upper rooms built one on top of another.
because they are one above another. And the ceiling of the lower upper room interposes against the impurity.
pardesak. A niche in the wall.

and it has closed doors, the house is pure. The pardesak interposes against the impurity. Some emend here according to the Tosefta (Oholot 7:14) that the house is impure because the way of impurity is to go out (Kesef Mishneh).
if the impurity was crushed in its floor or its walls or its roof. Of the pardesak, so that in effect the impurity is in the house's wall.
we regard the whole hole as if it were sealed. It is now like an ordinary wall, judged half and half (see above 24:4-5).
if the impurity was crushed within the structure. In the wall where the pardesaks are.
on the threshold of the house from outside. On the outer side of the step at the doorway of the house, for example where the threshold is not beneath the lintel of the house (Rosh, Oholot 12:8).
is judged half and half. Like crushed impurity beneath one of the walls of the house (see above 24:5).
it was stuck to the lintel. On its outer side. And the house is impure because its side is decreed on account of its underside (Tiferet Yisrael, ibid.; and see above 1:11).
and died within three days. From the time of eating, since within that period the impurity in its intestines still defiles (see above 20:4).

we regard the cavity of the impurity from his body etc.. We estimate the place where the impurity lies in the dog's body, and if that place is beneath the lintel, the house is impure (see Commentary on the Mishnah, Oholot 11:7).

if the head of the nefel became like a bundle of warp. The fetus managed to grow before death to the stage where its head reached the size of a bundle of warp threads (which are thinner than woof threads, and their bundle is smaller).

once the womb opened until the head was visible, the house became impure because of the fetus. Such an opening takes it out of the status of 'absorbed,' which does not defile (see above 20:2). But as long as the fetus has not rounded its head like a bundle, since its head is small and it can leave the womb without opening it, there is no opening here that takes it out of the status of absorbed (Sidrei Taharot, Oholot 117:2; compare Hilchot Bekhorot 4:13).
having difficulty giving birth. She is in labor.

for if her womb had opened there she could not have walked on her feet. And since she walked on her feet from house to house, there is no concern that the nefel's head already emerged in the first house.
carried by the armpits. Carried by her arms.
it is presumed that there is no afterbirth without a child. See also Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 10:14; Hilchot Bekhorot 4:10.

for it did not touch him from the time he came out into the air of the world. When the dead one comes out first, the living one does not follow after it but holds himself back inside, and as long as he remains in the womb the touch does not make him impure (see below, halakhah 12).
and if the living one came out first, he is impure. For a one-day-old infant receives impurity (above 1:14).
for he has no strength to hold himself back. Therefore he comes out immediately when the womb opens, after the living infant, and makes him impure.
as we explained. That a nefel defiles like an adult (above 2:1).
the midwife. The midwife.

once it came out into the prozdod. The neck of the womb that opens at childbirth (see Hilchot Issurei Bi'ah 5:3); a fetus that puts its head outside this place is considered as having come out and defiles by Torah law.
touch of the hidden places is not touch etc.. See above 1:3, 1:8.
and since it is within the intestines, one who touches it is pure. See Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 2:2.
